content/chapters/00-reading-guide.md::se.review_asset_definitions:
<!-- vale ai-tells.ExplainerHeadings = NO -->
# What the three papers establish {#ch:READING-GUIDE}
<!-- vale ai-tells.ExplainerHeadings = YES -->

<!-- vale ai-tells.CataphoricForecasting = NO -->
<!-- vale ai-tells.VerbTricolon = NO -->
The subject is neuroscience: how groups of nerve cells represent information used in memory, eye control, and navigation. The three papers examine mathematical models that store a quantity such as an angle, eye movements and neural activity recorded in macaque monkeys, and location-dependent neural activity recorded in rodents and bats. [They ask how activity can retain a value, how an internal fluctuation can move the eyes, and why a cell can respond at several separate locations.]{.key-statement}
<!-- vale ai-tells.VerbTricolon = YES -->
<!-- vale ai-tells.CataphoricForecasting = YES -->

## Variable neural signals must support reliable behavior {#sec:READING-FIELD}

<!-- vale ai-tells.BareHolds = NO -->
A remembered direction must remain useful after its cue disappears. The eyes must hold an angle while an animal looks at a target. A moving animal must keep track of where it is. These tasks depend on groups of [[**neuron**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}s, the brain's signaling cells]{.definition-explanation}, whose electrical signals are brief and variable. Computational and systems neuroscience studies how these cells and their interactions support such behavior. Mathematical models connect assumptions about cells and their interactions to predictions. Recordings test those predictions against neural activity and movement.
<!-- vale ai-tells.BareHolds = YES -->

## Persistent activity can still lose memory accuracy {#sec:READING-MEMORY}

Burak and Fiete (2012) study short-term memory for a continuous quantity, such as a direction or eye angle. A proposed mechanism is that interacting neurons keep activity going after the original input ends. [Yet the remembered value can change while the activity persists.]{.key-statement} The problem is to explain how the properties of the cells and their connections set the rate of this loss of accuracy.

<!-- vale ai-tells.VerbTricolon = NO -->
The authors analyze a network with a continuous family of persistent activity patterns, each representing a different value. Each cell sends signals at random times. They use an approximation for small fluctuations to derive how these signals move the stored value, compare the calculation with network simulations, and relate the motion to the best accuracy possible when estimating the stored value from those signals.
<!-- vale ai-tells.VerbTricolon = YES -->

<!-- vale ai-tells.EmDashUsage = NO -->
[Their central result is a lower bound: the uncertainty in reading the network's current value limits how slowly that value can wander.]{.key-statement} Under the model's assumptions, the variance of the memory error grows with storage time. Reading for longer also has diminishing benefit because the state continues moving during observation. This gives a benchmark for evaluating proposed memory circuits and their recall errors. It applies to the analyzed family of continuous-state memory models, with the required noise assumptions and no external signal anchoring the value. Chapters 3–6 develop the [diffusion calculation](../chapters/ch-memory-dynamics.html), its long-delay behavior, the [information bound](../chapters/ch-memory-information.html), and the limits of [readout](../chapters/ch-memory-readout.html).[^orientation-memory]
<!-- vale ai-tells.EmDashUsage = YES -->

## Eye drift points to a shared neural source {#sec:READING-EYE}

<!-- vale ai-tells.BareReaches = NO -->
<!-- vale ai-tells.FormalTransitions = NO -->
[Even while gaze is held on a stationary target, the eyes move smoothly and irregularly between brief, rapid movements. This smooth motion is called [**fixational drift**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}.]{.definition-explanation} It changes the image reaching the [[**retina**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}, the light-sensitive tissue at the back of the eye]{.definition-explanation}. Understanding its source is therefore part of understanding the visual signals the brain receives. [Ben-Shushan and colleagues (2022) ask whether the motion begins mainly in muscles or in neural commands sent to them.]{.key-statement}
<!-- vale ai-tells.FormalTransitions = YES -->
<!-- vale ai-tells.BareReaches = YES -->

They reanalyze recordings from 57 neurons that send commands to eye muscles in two macaques, paired with precise eye-position measurements. They first calibrate the relation between each cell's activity and larger eye movements. They then use it during fixation to compare the movement predicted from one cell with the measured movement. A separate circuit model tests whether a wandering stored eye-position command could explain the movement's amplitude and time dependence.

<!-- vale ai-tells.EmDashUsage = NO -->
<!-- vale ai-tells.ParallelStaccato = NO -->
For 350-millisecond intervals, their analysis estimates that about 82% of horizontal displacement variance comes from a common source before the final motor neurons, assuming the fitted movement relation also holds during fixation and the relevant noise contributions do not vary together. This supports a central neural contribution to drift. The memory-circuit model provides a possible explanation of that contribution, linking an internal storage error to observable behavior. The recordings do not uniquely locate the noise inside that memory circuit. Chapters 7–9 separate the [shared-drive inference](../chapters/ch-eye-drift.html), the [timing of drift](../chapters/ch-eye-timing.html), and the [proposed circuit mechanism](../chapters/ch-eye-circuit.html).[^orientation-eye]
<!-- vale ai-tells.ParallelStaccato = YES -->
<!-- vale ai-tells.EmDashUsage = YES -->

## Smooth random maps explain the variety of place fields {#sec:READING-PLACE}

<!-- vale ai-tells.EmptyPaddingStacked = NO -->
<!-- vale ai-tells.FormalTransitions = NO -->
[A [**place cell**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} in the [**hippocampus**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}, a brain region involved in memory and navigation, becomes more active in particular locations.]{.definition-explanation} [Each connected region of elevated activity is a [**place field**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}.]{.definition-explanation} Small environments encouraged a picture of one smooth field per cell. Larger environments reveal multiple fields with widely varying sizes and shapes. [Mainali, Azeredo da Silveira, and Burak (2025) ask whether one statistical account can explain this variety across species and spatial dimensions.]{.key-statement}
<!-- vale ai-tells.FormalTransitions = YES -->
<!-- vale ai-tells.EmptyPaddingStacked = YES -->

Their model gives each cell a smooth random function of location and allows activity where that function exceeds a threshold. The authors derive predictions for the resulting regions, simulate the model, and compare it with existing rodent and bat recordings from one-, two- and three-dimensional environments. Parameters fitted to field sizes and their spatial arrangement also support further tests of field shapes and connectedness.

<!-- vale ai-tells.EmDashUsage = NO -->
<!-- vale ai-tells.ParallelStaccato = NO -->
The model explains different size distributions across dimensions and predicts additional features, such as multiple peaks within a field and inactive holes surrounded by activity. This makes irregular spatial responses quantitatively understandable and supports a common statistical description across the examined settings. Such statistics can arise when cells combine many inputs through largely random connections. The study does not directly measure those connections. Chapters 10–12 develop the [spatial model](../chapters/ch-place-fields.html), its [size and shape predictions](../chapters/ch-place-sizes.html), and the [tests and circuit interpretation](../chapters/ch-place-tests.html). They distinguish exact predictions, limiting approximations and empirical comparisons.[^orientation-place]
<!-- vale ai-tells.ParallelStaccato = YES -->
<!-- vale ai-tells.EmDashUsage = YES -->

<!-- vale ai-tells.CataphoricForecasting = NO -->
<!-- vale ai-tells.FormalTransitions = NO -->
<!-- vale ai-tells.ServesAsDodge = NO -->
<!-- vale ai-tells.VerbTricolon = NO -->
The three contributions therefore have different meanings: a mathematical constraint on memory models, evidence about the source of eye movement, and a statistical explanation of spatial activity. Together they show how a representation can be described, maintained and related to behavior. Combining all three in one biological circuit remains a further research question, developed in [Chapter 13](../chapters/ch-synthesis.html).
<!-- vale ai-tells.VerbTricolon = YES -->
<!-- vale ai-tells.ServesAsDodge = YES -->
<!-- vale ai-tells.FormalTransitions = YES -->
<!-- vale ai-tells.CataphoricForecasting = YES -->

## Starting knowledge and reading paths {#sec:READING-START}

<!-- vale ai-tells.AnthropomorphicCognition = NO -->
The guide assumes undergraduate calculus, basic probability, and linear algebra. Neuroscience terms and the required stochastic-process, information, filtering, and random-field ideas are taught where needed. The reading path builds from the signals to the models and then their tests:
<!-- vale ai-tells.AnthropomorphicCognition = YES -->

  <!-- vale ai-tells.EmDashUsage = NO -->
- **Chapters 1–2:** establish [neural signals and variability](../chapters/ch-foundations.html), then [persistence and accumulated error](../chapters/ch-persistence.html).
  <!-- vale ai-tells.EmDashUsage = YES -->
  <!-- vale ai-tells.EmDashUsage = NO -->
  <!-- vale ai-tells.VerbTricolon = NO -->
- **Chapters 3–6:** derive memory diffusion, its long-delay behavior, the information bound, and readout.
  <!-- vale ai-tells.VerbTricolon = YES -->
  <!-- vale ai-tells.EmDashUsage = YES -->
  <!-- vale ai-tells.EmDashUsage = NO -->
- **Chapters 7–9:** follow the eye study from shared-drive evidence through timing to a circuit model.
  <!-- vale ai-tells.EmDashUsage = YES -->
  <!-- vale ai-tells.VerbTricolon = NO -->
- **Chapters 10–12:** develop spatial maps, their size predictions, and tests of their shapes and possible origins.
  <!-- vale ai-tells.VerbTricolon = YES -->
- **Chapter 13:** connect the results and compare related work.

<!-- vale ai-tells.EmptyPadding = NO -->
For a path focused on particular papers:
<!-- vale ai-tells.EmptyPadding = YES -->

- **Memory and eye drift:** follow chapters 1 through 9 in order.
  <!-- vale ai-tells.EmDashUsage = NO -->
- **Place fields:** read the two foundations chapters and then chapters 10–12. The spatial calculation does not require the readout derivation in chapter 6.
  <!-- vale ai-tells.EmDashUsage = YES -->

The Glossary gives short definitions for lookup after their first explanation. The References section gives full source details. The original paper figures are discussed by number and can be inspected in the linked PDFs.

After the foundations, the [guide map](../chapters/ch-persistence.html#fig-foundations-paper-map) shows the three paper questions together.

On a first reading, follow the main text, figures, assumptions, and results. The expandable notes preserve longer calculations and extensions. Open one when you want to check the steps behind a result. The explanations needed for the next section remain in the main text.

## Neural mechanisms and mathematical derivations answer different questions {#sec:READING-MECHANISM-MATH}

<!-- vale ai-tells.EmDashUsage = NO -->
Chapters 3–6 explain [how interacting neurons can retain a value while random spike timing changes it.]{.key-statement} Their treatment of the Burak and Fiete appendix separates three parts of each substantial topic:
<!-- vale ai-tells.EmDashUsage = YES -->

   <!-- vale ai-tells.VerbTricolon = NO -->
1. **Neural mechanism:** which cells and signals interact, what changes, and which features are assumptions of the model. For readout, this part also states what an observer can measure and which value it must estimate.
   <!-- vale ai-tells.VerbTricolon = YES -->
   <!-- vale ai-tells.VerbTricolon = NO -->
2. **Mathematical derivation:** the general tool, its conditions, and the calculation after neural quantities are assigned to the symbols.
   <!-- vale ai-tells.VerbTricolon = YES -->
3. **Interpretation:** what the result predicts about memory or readout, and what its assumptions leave unresolved.

<!-- vale ai-tells.StackedAnaphora = NO -->
[An equation that specifies how a cell responds belongs to the model. A derivation works out what follows from that choice.]{.key-statement}
<!-- vale ai-tells.StackedAnaphora = YES -->

<!-- vale ai-tells.FormalTransitions = NO -->
For example, a spike can disturb several cells' activity. The circuit's interactions remove some changes, while others leave the represented angle displaced. Linear algebra calculates which part survives. Probability gives the spread of that displacement. The result then predicts how quickly memory errors accumulate in this model. The mathematical tools also apply to other systems, but this neural prediction depends on the circuit and spike statistics used in the calculation.
<!-- vale ai-tells.FormalTransitions = YES -->

The same distinction matters for readout. A calculation of the best possible estimate sets a benchmark under specified access to neural signals. Establishing that an animal's neurons implement the assumed computation requires separate evidence.

<!-- vale ai-tells.FigurativeHolds = NO -->
For a first conceptual pass, read the mechanism, inspect the displayed result and its variables, then read the interpretation. Follow the mathematical derivation when you want to understand why the result holds or calculate with it. Assumptions remain part of both readings.
<!-- vale ai-tells.FigurativeHolds = YES -->

<!-- vale ai-tells.AnthropomorphicCognition = NO -->
The [PNAS appendix](https://www.pnas.org/action/downloadSupplement?doi=10.1073%2Fpnas.1117386109&file=Appendix.pdf) supplies both neural-model choices and mathematical arguments. This map links its seven sections to the guide's explanations. Page links open the local copy. The guide sometimes uses an equivalent teaching derivation and identifies source inconsistencies beside the affected calculation.
<!-- vale ai-tells.AnthropomorphicCognition = YES -->

{{block:tbl:READING-APPENDIX}}

## How to interpret the calculations and evidence {#sec:READING-SCOPE}

<!-- vale ai-tells.AnthropomorphicCognition = NO -->
Examples chosen for the guide distinguish independent from shared fluctuations, complete from limited access to neural signals, and exact formulas from approximations for rare fields. Their numbers are checked separately from the published experimental measurements. A teaching reconstruction is labeled when its simplified model differs from the paper's full model.
<!-- vale ai-tells.AnthropomorphicCognition = YES -->

<!-- vale ai-tells.RestatementMarkers = NO -->
The guide explains how to interpret the experiments and their figures. It does not rerun the original animal recordings, data processing, or full neural-network simulations. [A successful numerical check of a probability identity is different from an independent reproduction of a paper's empirical result.]{.key-statement} Related work is selected to clarify the assumptions and alternatives rather than to claim an exhaustive literature search.
<!-- vale ai-tells.RestatementMarkers = YES -->

Throughout the guide, $D$ denotes the [[**diffusion coefficient**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}, which sets how quickly uncertainty spreads]{.definition-explanation}. In the basic one-dimensional model, $D$ is constant, neither direction is favored, and no boundary limits the motion. Its [[**mean squared displacement**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} (MSD), the average squared change in the represented coordinate after elapsed time $t$]{.definition-explanation}, is $2Dt$. [Chapter 2](../chapters/ch-persistence.html#sec-foundations-diffusion) explains this model and its assumptions.

The other recurring symbols are:

- $d$: spatial dimension.
- $\theta$: the represented coordinate in the memory chapters.
- $q$: the normalized threshold in the place-field chapters, called $\theta$ in that paper.
- $C$: the spatial covariance in the place-field chapters.

## The original papers {#sec:READING-PAPERS}

The copies are the published versions. Supporting information is linked separately.

  <!-- vale ai-tells.EmDashUsage = NO -->
- **Burak and Fiete (2012):** [Paper PDF](../papers/burak-fiete-2012-persistent-activity.pdf) and [20-page supporting information PDF](../papers/burak-fiete-2012-persistent-activity-si.pdf). *Fundamental limits on persistent activity in networks of noisy neurons*. PNAS, 109(43), 17645–17650. [Published DOI](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1117386109). The local main PDF uses the six-page Early Edition layout, so PDF page locators run from 1 to 6.

# Eye drift points to a shared neural drive {#ch:EYE-DRIFT}

<!-- vale ai-tells.EmptyPadding = NO -->
Looking steadily at a small spot does not hold the eye perfectly still. [Between brief, rapid movements called [**microsaccades**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}, the eye makes a small, smooth, irregular movement called fixational drift.]{.definition-explanation} [Does this movement begin as noise in the muscles, or does the brain send a changing command to them?]{.key-statement} Ben-Shushan and colleagues answer this in two stages. Their recordings support a large shared drive upstream of the motor neurons. Their model then proposes a particular source: random motion of the eye position stored in a memory circuit.[^p2-question]
<!-- vale ai-tells.EmptyPadding = YES -->

This distinction connects the previous chapters to a measurement outside the brain. A memory coordinate can diffuse inside a neural network, but the movement produced by that coordinate also depends on the muscles and the mechanics of the eye. We need to follow the signal through those stages before comparing a neural diffusion law with an eye trajectory.

A recording from one motor neuron becomes useful for this comparison only after its spikes and the eye's movement can be expressed on the same scale. The larger movements provide that calibration. Applying it during fixation then lets us ask whether independent motor noise could explain the observed relationship, and estimate the shared contribution under explicit gain and independence assumptions.

review_metadata.title: Eye drift points to a shared neural drive
review_metadata.purpose: Even when a monkey looks at a stationary spot, its eyes drift slightly. This chapter explains how paired measurements of eye angle and the firing of neurons that command eye muscles support a shared neural source of that drift, before considering a particular circuit mechanism.

section_list.title: From stored eye position to muscle action
section_list.summary: The eye needs an ongoing command to maintain a position. A brief command to move is therefore insufficient: after the movement, a circuit must maintain activity representing the new position. The [**oculomotor integrator**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} is the neural circuit that performs this storage. “Integrator” refers to turning a movement command into a lasting position signal. In the proposed mechanism, the continuous attractor described in the [foundations](ch-persistence.html#sec-foundations-attractor) and [network model](ch-memory-dynamics.html#sec-memory-spikes) stores horizontal eye position. Noise moves the stored value along that attractor.[^p2-pathway]

section_list.title: The recordings pair one motor neuron with movement at a time
section_list.summary: The authors reanalyzed earlier experiments in two male rhesus macaques. With their heads held still, the monkeys first looked at a stationary spot of light on a monitor and then followed the moving spot. A wire search coil on one eye measured the eye's angle while an electrode recorded one neuron's spikes. There were 57 identified OMNs. Each recording paired one OMN with eye movement. There were no simultaneous recordings of multiple OMNs. Thus the analysis cannot directly measure the covariance between two recorded motor neurons.[^p2-recordings][^p2-single]

section_list.title: A calibrated filter predicts eye position from one cell's spikes
section_list.summary: To ask how much eye movement is shared with a neuron, it helps to express both signals in degrees. The paper reverses the fitted relationship: a cell's spike train becomes the input, and its prediction of eye position becomes the output. This operation is an inverse of the movement-to-rate fit, rather than a new fit to small drift residuals.

section_list.title: The measured correlation challenges independent motor noise alone
section_list.summary: A correlation of 0.17 does not immediately tell us how much motion comes from the common command. First we can ask a more limited question: could all the motion come from independent motor neuron fluctuations?

# Eye drift points to a shared neural drive {#ch:EYE-DRIFT} Looking steadily at a small spot does not hold the eye perfectly still. [Between brief, rapid movements called [**microsaccades**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}, the eye makes a small, smooth, irregular movement called fixational drift.]{.definition-explanation} [Does this movement begin as noise in the muscles, or does the brain send a changing command to them?]{.key-statement} Ben-Shushan and colleagues answer this in two stages. Their recordings support a large shared drive upstream of the motor neurons. Their model then proposes a particular source: random motion of the eye position stored in a memory circuit.[^p2-question] This distinction connects the previous chapters to a measurement outside the brain. A memory coordinate can diffuse inside a neural network, but the movement produced by that coordinate also depends on the muscles and the mechanics of the eye. We need to follow the signal through those stages before comparing a neural diffusion law with an eye trajectory. A recording from one motor neuron becomes useful for this comparison only after its spikes and the eye's movement can be expressed on the same scale. The larger movements provide that calibration. Applying it during fixation then lets us ask whether independent motor noise could explain the observed relationship, and estimate the shared contribution under explicit gain and independence assumptions. ## From stored eye position to muscle action {#sec:EYE-PATHWAY} The eye needs an ongoing command to maintain a position. A brief command to move is therefore insufficient: after the movement, a circuit must maintain activity representing the new position. [The [**oculomotor integrator**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} is the neural circuit that performs this storage. “Integrator” refers to turning a movement command into a lasting position signal.]{.definition-explanation} In the proposed mechanism, the continuous attractor described in the [foundations](ch-persistence.html#sec-foundations-attractor) and [network model](ch-memory-dynamics.html#sec-memory-spikes) stores horizontal eye position. Noise moves the stored value along that attractor.[^p2-pathway] [The signal reaches [**ocular motoneurons (OMNs)**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}, neurons whose spikes activate the eye muscles.]{.definition-explanation} [The recordings came from the [**abducens nucleus**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}, a group of brainstem neurons that includes OMNs activating the lateral rectus muscle, which turns the eye outward.]{.definition-explanation} Other neurons in that nucleus carry signals to other neurons rather than directly to muscle. The study separated these cell types by how their firing changed with eye position and movement. [Finally, the muscles and the mechanical properties of the eye, together called the [**ocular plant**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}, turn neural activity into movement.]{.definition-explanation}[^p2-recordings]
Original paper figure: Ben-Shushan et al. (2022), Extended Data Figure 6
{{block:fig:PAPER-EYE-ED6}}
There are three possible contributions to an observed drift: - A changing shared command sent to many OMNs. - Private spike variability in individual OMNs. - Variability after those neurons, including muscle and measurement noise. [Private spike fluctuations can partly cancel when many neurons act together. A common command survives this averaging.]{.key-statement} This is why the noisy activity of one neuron can reveal a source that dominates the much smoother eye movement. ## The recordings pair one motor neuron with movement at a time {#sec:EYE-RECORDINGS} The authors reanalyzed earlier experiments in two male rhesus macaques. With their heads held still, the monkeys first looked at a stationary spot of light on a monitor and then followed the moving spot. A wire search coil on one eye measured the eye's angle while an electrode recorded one neuron's spikes. There were 57 identified OMNs. [Each recording paired one OMN with eye movement. There were no simultaneous recordings of multiple OMNs. Thus the analysis cannot directly measure the covariance between two recorded motor neurons.]{.key-statement}[^p2-recordings][^p2-single] The initial stationary target was followed by 500–700 ms of required fixation before the target stepped and began moving. Neural voltage was sampled at 25 kHz and eye position at 1 kHz. The authors detected microsaccades using eye speed and acceleration, removed 30 ms on each side of them, and manually checked the remaining segments. For the main displacement analysis, segments shorter than 350 ms were excluded and longer ones were split into nonoverlapping 350 ms pieces. There were 302 such pieces per cell on average, with different counts across cells. These repeated observations improve estimates within two animals. They do not create 57 independent animal samples.[^p2-segments]
Original paper figure: Ben-Shushan et al. (2022), Extended Data Figure 7
{{block:fig:PAPER-EYE-ED7}}
The large movements have a useful role even though the scientific question concerns tiny drifts. They produce enough rate change to estimate how each cell's activity depends on eye movement. The fitted relationship is then applied during fixation. This transfer is an assumption to examine, because an incorrect gain during drift would change the inferred common variance. Gain is the scale that converts a change in one signal into a change in the other.
{{block:fig:EYE-PHYSICAL-AND-RECORDED}}
## A fitted model links movement to firing rate {#sec:EYE-FORWARD-FIT} Position alone does not predict a motor neuron's activity during a movement. At the same position, firing can differ when the eye is moving or accelerating. The paper therefore fits $$ \widehat f(t)=k[E(t+\Delta t)-E_T] +r\dot E(t+\Delta t)+m\ddot E(t+\Delta t). $$ Here $E$ is horizontal eye position in degrees and $\widehat f$ is predicted firing rate in spikes/s. The position threshold $E_T$ sets where the position term reaches zero. The coefficients have units $$ [k]=\frac{\text{spikes}}{\text{s}\,\text{deg}},\qquad [r]=\frac{\text{spikes}}{\text{deg}},\qquad [m]=\frac{\text{spikes}\,\text{s}}{\text{deg}}. $$ Multiplying by position, velocity, and acceleration gives spikes/s in all three terms. The position term describes ongoing firing associated with holding the eye at an angle. The velocity term allows a different rate while the eye passes through that same angle. The acceleration term allows another change while its velocity changes. Thus $k$, $r$, and $m$ describe different demands on the motor signal. They are fitted coefficients of the combined neural and mechanical relationship. In particular, $m$ is not a direct measurement of the eye's mass. The delay $\Delta t$ is in seconds: firing at time $t$ predicts movement at the later time $t+\Delta t$ for a positive neural lead. This is the paper's Eq. 2, including its threshold and time shift.[^p2-forward] The observed rate $f(t)$ was estimated as the inverse of the interval between successive spikes, constant between those spikes. For each cell, the authors minimized the sum of squared rate errors, $$ L=\sum_{a=1}^{n_{\rm trials}}\sum_{t_j\in[0,T_a]} \left[f_a(t_j)-\widehat f_a(t_j;k,r,m,\Delta t,E_T)\right]^2. $$ $a$ labels trials and $T_a$ is trial duration. This is Eq. 3 with the trial count renamed so that it cannot be confused with a neuron count. Fits used full trials, including fixation and pursuit. To predict a trial's rate, that trial was left out of the parameter fit. Acceleration was estimated from velocity after local polynomial smoothing over 21 ms. Trials in which the rate fell below 20 Hz were discarded: the linear formula is intended for active cells above firing threshold, whereas firing cannot become negative.[^p2-forward] During fixation, the authors subtracted each segment's mean firing rate, joined the segments, and compared observed and predicted rate fluctuations. Figure 1c illustrates a weak relationship for one cell. Fig. 1d shows a positive population effect. The one sided test asks whether the mean correlation is positive, compared with a zero-mean reference. [Its [**p value**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} is the probability, under that reference, of a test statistic at least as large as observed.]{.definition-explanation} Across 57 cells it gave $p=3\times10^{-9}$. A weak single cell relationship is expected here because the tiny movement produces small rate changes against much larger spike variability. This is the first evidence of a relationship, before any estimate of the fraction of common motion.[^p2-rate-result]
Original paper figure: Ben-Shushan et al. (2022), Figure 1
{{block:fig:PAPER-EYE-1}}
## A calibrated filter predicts eye position from one cell's spikes {#sec:EYE-INVERSE-FILTER} To ask how much eye movement is shared with a neuron, it helps to express both signals in degrees. [The paper reverses the fitted relationship: a cell's spike train becomes the input, and its prediction of eye position becomes the output. This operation is an inverse of the movement-to-rate fit, rather than a new fit to small drift residuals.]{.key-statement} Let $x(t)=E(t)-E_T$. Ignoring the time shift for a moment, the deterministic relation is $$ m\ddot x+r\dot x+kx=f. $$ [A [**causal filter**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} computes its present output from present and past input. For the equation above, its [**impulse response**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} $h_0(u)$ is the position response to one instantaneous spike at time zero.]{.definition-explanation} To factor the equation, consider a time component $e^{pt}$: differentiation multiplies it by $p$. The algebraic ratio of output to input for that component is $$ H_0(p)=\frac{1}{mp^2+rp+k} =\frac{1}{m(p+1/\tau_+)(p+1/\tau_-)}. $$ Factoring the quadratic gives the slow and fast decay times $$ \tau_+=\frac{2}{r/m-\sqrt{(r/m)^2-4k/m}},\qquad \tau_-=\frac{2}{r/m+\sqrt{(r/m)^2-4k/m}}. $$ These are the paired signs in the paper's Eq. 7, with $\tau_+>\tau_-$ when $k,r,m>0$ and $r^2>4km$. Under these conditions both components decay without oscillation. At rest, the inverse equation gives $x=f/k$: with the threshold fixed, doubling $k$ halves the position offset predicted from the same steady firing rate. During a change, $r$ and $m$ also affect the response through the two timescales. This is a consequence of the fitted relationship, not evidence that changing one recorded neuron's rate alone sets eye position. The same factorization gives two useful identities: $$ \tau_+\tau_-=\frac{m}{k},\qquad \tau_++\tau_-=\frac{r}{k}. $$ The corresponding impulse response is $$ h_0(u)=\frac{\Theta(u)}{m}\, \frac{\tau_+\tau_-}{\tau_+-\tau_-} \left(e^{-u/\tau_+}-e^{-u/\tau_-}\right). $$ $\Theta(u)$ is zero for $u<0$ and one for $u>0$, which makes the response zero before the input. Restoring the fitted neural lead delays this response: $h(u)=h_0(u-\Delta t)$. Write the spike train as $\xi(t)=\sum_j\delta(t-t_j)$, where $\delta$ is an ideal instantaneous impulse of unit area, so integration over one spike counts one event. The prediction is $$ \widehat E(t)=E_T+\int_{-\infty}^{t}h(t-v)\xi(v)\,dv =E_T+\sum_j h(t-t_j). $$ These expressions reproduce Eqs. 4–6, including the factor $\tau_+\tau_-/m$ and the delay. [The [**convolution**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} integral adds the responses to all past spikes.]{.definition-explanation} With spike count treated as a count, $\xi$ has units spikes/s and $h$ has units degrees/spike. Each spike contributes a decaying position response. Adding those responses produces degrees.[^p2-inversion] ::: {.publisher-clarification-note .publisher-fold-always title="Derivation: the weights of the two decaying responses"} We can obtain the response to a spike directly from the differential equation. After the spike, the input is zero, and each of the two exponentials solves the remaining homogeneous equation. Write their combination as $$ h_0(u)=A e^{-u/\tau_+}+B e^{-u/\tau_-},\qquad u>0. $$ To find $A$ and $B$, treat the spike as a short pulse of unit area and shrink its duration to zero. The position change during that pulse tends to zero, so $h_0(0^+)=0$. Integrating $m h_0''+r h_0'+k h_0$ across the pulse gives $m h_0'(0^+)=1$: the velocity changes by $1/m$, while position and velocity before the causal response are zero. Therefore $$ A+B=0,\qquad -\frac{A}{\tau_+}-\frac{B}{\tau_-}=\frac1m. $$ Substituting $B=-A$ gives $A(1/\tau_- -1/\tau_+)=1/m$, hence $A=\tau_+\tau_-/[m(\tau_+-\tau_-)]$. Making the response zero before the spike gives the impulse response $h_0(u)$. ::: For a constructed example, take $k=4$ spikes/(s deg), $\tau_+=0.120$ s, and $\tau_-=0.005$ s. The identities above require $r=0.500$ spikes/deg and $m=0.00240$ spikes s/deg. Then $$ h_0(u)=2.174\left(e^{-u/0.120}-e^{-u/0.005}\right) \ \text{deg/spike},\quad u>0, $$ and its area is $2.174(0.120-0.005)=0.250$ deg s/spike, equal to $1/k$. A steady rate of 80 spikes/s predicts an offset of 20 degrees above $E_T$. This checks the gain and the time constants. ::: {.publisher-clarification-note .publisher-fold-always title="Check: static gain and equal decay times"} The kernel's area checks its normalization: $$ \int_0^\infty h_0(u)\,du =\frac{\tau_+\tau_-}{m(\tau_+-\tau_-)}(\tau_+-\tau_-) =\frac1k. $$ Thus a constant input rate $f_0$ predicts $E_T+f_0/k$, exactly the static forward relation. A kernel with unit area would give the wrong conversion unless $k$ had already been absorbed into the input. When the two decay times coincide, $r^2=4km$, the limit is $h_0(u)=\Theta(u)u e^{-u/\tau}/m$. The distinct exponential formula is used for the fitted responses in the paper. ::: Figure 2a–b shows typical fitted times of about 5 ms and 120 ms. Figure 2c shows that a single cell's reconstructed drift is much noisier than the measured movement. Across 350 ms displacement pairs, the mean Pearson correlation was $\langle R\rangle=0.17\pm0.02$, [where the error is the [**standard error of the mean (SEM)**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}. SEM estimates uncertainty in the across-cell mean, rather than the spread of individual cells or uncertainty across animals.]{.definition-explanation} The one sided test gave $p=3.8\times10^{-12}$. Shuffling which measured segment was paired with which spike prediction centered the comparison near zero. Here and below $\langle\cdot\rangle$ over cells means a population average.[^p2-correlation]
Original paper figure: Ben-Shushan et al. (2022), Figure 2
{{block:fig:PAPER-EYE-2}}
## The measured correlation challenges independent motor noise alone {#sec:EYE-SHARED-VARIANCE} A correlation of 0.17 does not immediately tell us how much motion comes from the common command. First we can ask a more limited question: could all the motion come from independent motor neuron fluctuations? For a centered displacement $Y$ and one centered prediction $X$, the best linear prediction $bX$ minimizes $\operatorname{Var}(Y-bX)$. Differentiating with respect to $b$ gives $b=\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)/\operatorname{Var}(X)$. Its explained fraction of variance is $$ \frac{b^2\operatorname{Var}(X)}{\operatorname{Var}(Y)} =\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)^2}{\operatorname{Var}(X)\operatorname{Var}(Y)} =R^2. $$ [This is the [**coefficient of determination**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} for a linear prediction with a fitted gain.]{.definition-explanation} It does not assert that the raw, unscaled position predictor itself has a small squared error. Suppose there are $N_m$ independent single neuron predictors $X_i$. Standardize each to variance one and also standardize $Y$. Independence makes the $X_i$ uncorrelated, so the residual after using them all has variance $$ \operatorname{Var}\left(Y-\sum_i R_iX_i\right) =1-2\sum_iR_i^2+\sum_iR_i^2 =1-\sum_iR_i^2\ge0. $$ Consequently $\sum_iR_i^2\le1$, and an average neuron explains at most $1/N_m$. This proves the bound used in Supplementary Eq. S1. It does not require equal muscle effects from all neurons. Applying it to the sampled cells does require their average explanatory power to represent the relevant motor population.[^p2-independent-bound] The authors avoid directly averaging noisy squared correlations. Instead, $$ \langle R^2\rangle-\langle R\rangle^2=\operatorname{Var}(R)\ge0, \qquad \langle R^2\rangle\ge(0.17)^2=0.0289. $$ [Thus the estimated mean correlation implies an average explained fraction of at least about 2.9%. For 1,000 independently contributing motor neurons, the bound would be 0.1%. For several thousand it is smaller. The mismatch argues against independent OMN noise as the sole source.]{.key-statement} Shared fluctuations can allow many cells to explain the same part of the movement, so their explained fractions can overlap.[^p2-independent-bound] This step finds shared variation. Locating its source upstream also uses a biological premise: the private variability generated within OMNs is taken to be independent across cells. The paper supports that premise using anatomical and stimulation studies indicating little local recurrent coupling in the relevant motor nuclei. It was not tested by simultaneous recordings in this data set. Common inputs can correlate the total activity of OMNs even when their privately generated spike noise is independent.[^p2-independence] ## Calibrated covariance estimates the common share of movement variance {#sec:EYE-CHI} The variance bound establishes that a shared signal exists, but leaves its size open. The next calculation uses the inverse filter’s calibrated gain in degrees. For one 350 ms interval, write the measured displacement and the single cell prediction as $$ Y=\delta E=C+\eta,\qquad X=\delta\widehat E=C+\epsilon, $$ where $C=\delta E_C$ is the common upstream contribution, $\eta$ combines motor neuron, muscle, and measurement contributions to measured displacement, and $\epsilon$ is the prediction error from the individual cell. All are displacement variables in degrees. The calculation assumes: - The common contribution enters both signals with unit gain, meaning the same one-for-one displacement scale. - $C,\eta,\epsilon$ are pairwise uncorrelated to the required accuracy. Expanding the covariance shows why those assumptions matter: $$ \operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=\operatorname{Var}(C) +\operatorname{Cov}(C,\eta)+\operatorname{Cov}(\epsilon,C) +\operatorname{Cov}(\epsilon,\eta) \simeq\operatorname{Var}(C). $$ The common fraction is therefore estimated by $$ \chi=\frac{\operatorname{Var}(C)}{\operatorname{Var}(Y)} \simeq\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)}{\operatorname{Var}(Y)}. $$ These are Eqs. 11–15 in displacement form. The gain assumption requires that the relation calibrated during larger movements still applies during drift. There is also a small covariance between $\epsilon$ and $\eta$, because the recorded neuron's private spikes contribute both to its predictor and to actual eye motion. The paper neglects this contribution as order $1/N_m$ under its many neuron model.[^p2-chi-method] Correlation divides the same covariance by a different denominator: $$ R=\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)}{\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(X)\operatorname{Var}(Y)}}, \qquad \chi\simeq R\sqrt{\frac{\operatorname{Var}(X)}{\operatorname{Var}(Y)}}. $$ [Large private noise in a cell inflates $\operatorname{Var}(X)$ and makes $R$ small. It need not make the common contribution to the real movement small, because many independent private contributions average down there.]{.key-statement}
**Example: correlation 0.17 with a common fraction 0.82.** These numbers are constructed to expose the distinction, not extracted from individual cells. Take independent centered variables with $$ \operatorname{Var}(C)=0.00820\ \text{deg}^2,\quad \operatorname{Var}(\eta)=0.00180\ \text{deg}^2,\quad \operatorname{Var}(\epsilon)=0.22446\ \text{deg}^2. $$ Then $\operatorname{Var}(Y)=0.01000$, $\operatorname{Var}(X)=0.23266$, and $\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=0.00820$, all in deg$^2$. It follows that $$ R=\frac{0.00820}{\sqrt{0.01000\times0.23266}}\simeq0.170, \qquad \chi=\frac{0.00820}{0.01000}=0.820. $$ One cell explains $R^2\simeq2.89\%$ of displacement variance after linear rescaling, while the common signal supplies 82% of actual displacement variance. The larger, poorly predicted part of the single cell signal is private prediction noise.
{{block:fig:EYE-SHARED-PRIVATE-VARIANCE}}
The bars use the same physical scale, so the equal common pieces have equal lengths. See [Shared and private variability, Eqs. 11–15, p. 10](../papers/ben-shushan-2022-fixational-drift.pdf#page=10).
In the experiment, each cell gives a noisy estimate $\chi_i$, and those estimates can lie outside $[0,1]$. The underlying variance fraction remains in that interval under the model, but the sample covariance need not. The paper estimates each standard error $\Delta\chi_i$ mainly from covariance uncertainty, treating the measured displacement variance in the denominator as comparatively well determined. It then uses inverse variance weighting: $$ w_i=\frac{1}{(\Delta\chi_i)^2},\qquad \widehat\chi=\frac{\sum_iw_i\chi_i}{\sum_iw_i},\qquad \sigma_{\widehat\chi}=\left(\sum_iw_i\right)^{-1/2}. $$ To see the weighting, let normalized weights $a_i$ sum to one. Independent errors give variance $\sum_i a_i^2(\Delta\chi_i)^2$ for $\sum_i a_i\chi_i$. Minimizing this subject to $\sum_i a_i=1$ gives $a_i\propto1/(\Delta\chi_i)^2$ and the error above. The paper additionally assumes approximately normal errors around a common value. The last expression is a propagated estimation error under those assumptions. It does not measure variation across animals or uncertainty in the gain and independence assumptions. ## From stored eye position to muscle action {#sec:EYE-PATHWAY} The eye needs an ongoing command to maintain a position. A brief command to move is therefore insufficient: after the movement, a circuit must maintain activity representing the new position. [The [**oculomotor integrator**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} is the neural circuit that performs this storage. “Integrator” refers to turning a movement command into a lasting position signal.]{.definition-explanation} In the proposed mechanism, the continuous attractor described in the [foundations](ch-persistence.html#sec-foundations-attractor) and [network model](ch-memory-dynamics.html#sec-memory-spikes) stores horizontal eye position. Noise moves the stored value along that attractor.[^p2-pathway] [The signal reaches [**ocular motoneurons (OMNs)**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}, neurons whose spikes activate the eye muscles.]{.definition-explanation} [The recordings came from the [**abducens nucleus**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}, a group of brainstem neurons that includes OMNs activating the lateral rectus muscle, which turns the eye outward.]{.definition-explanation} Other neurons in that nucleus carry signals to other neurons rather than directly to muscle. The study separated these cell types by how their firing changed with eye position and movement. [Finally, the muscles and the mechanical properties of the eye, together called the [**ocular plant**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}, turn neural activity into movement.]{.definition-explanation}[^p2-recordings]
Original paper figure: Ben-Shushan et al. (2022), Extended Data Figure 6
{{block:fig:PAPER-EYE-ED6}}
There are three possible contributions to an observed drift: - A changing shared command sent to many OMNs. - Private spike variability in individual OMNs. - Variability after those neurons, including muscle and measurement noise. [Private spike fluctuations can partly cancel when many neurons act together. A common command survives this averaging.]{.key-statement} This is why the noisy activity of one neuron can reveal a source that dominates the much smoother eye movement.

review_metadata.title: Eye drift points to a shared neural drive
review_metadata.purpose: Even when a monkey looks at a stationary spot, its eyes drift slightly. This chapter explains how paired measurements of eye angle and the firing of neurons that command eye muscles support a shared neural source of that drift, before considering a particular circuit mechanism.

section_list.title: From stored eye position to muscle action
section_list.summary: The eye needs an ongoing command to maintain a position. A brief command to move is therefore insufficient: after the movement, a circuit must maintain activity representing the new position. The [**oculomotor integrator**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} is the neural circuit that performs this storage. “Integrator” refers to turning a movement command into a lasting position signal. In the proposed mechanism, the continuous attractor described in the [foundations](ch-persistence.html#sec-foundations-attractor) and [network model](ch-memory-dynamics.html#sec-memory-spikes) stores horizontal eye position. Noise moves the stored value along that attractor.[^p2-pathway]

section_list.title: The recordings pair one motor neuron with movement at a time

# Eye drift points to a shared neural drive {#ch:EYE-DRIFT} Looking steadily at a small spot does not hold the eye perfectly still. [Between brief, rapid movements called [**microsaccades**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}, the eye makes a small, smooth, irregular movement called fixational drift.]{.definition-explanation} [Does this movement begin as noise in the muscles, or does the brain send a changing command to them?]{.key-statement} Ben-Shushan and colleagues answer this in two stages. Their recordings support a large shared drive upstream of the motor neurons. Their model then proposes a particular source: random motion of the eye position stored in a memory circuit.[^p2-question] This distinction connects the previous chapters to a measurement outside the brain. A memory coordinate can diffuse inside a neural network, but the movement produced by that coordinate also depends on the muscles and the mechanics of the eye. We need to follow the signal through those stages before comparing a neural diffusion law with an eye trajectory. A recording from one motor neuron becomes useful for this comparison only after its spikes and the eye's movement can be expressed on the same scale. The larger movements provide that calibration. Applying it during fixation then lets us ask whether independent motor noise could explain the observed relationship, and estimate the shared contribution under explicit gain and independence assumptions. ## From stored eye position to muscle action {#sec:EYE-PATHWAY} The eye needs an ongoing command to maintain a position. A brief command to move is therefore insufficient: after the movement, a circuit must maintain activity representing the new position. [The [**oculomotor integrator**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} is the neural circuit that performs this storage. “Integrator” refers to turning a movement command into a lasting position signal.]{.definition-explanation} In the proposed mechanism, the continuous attractor described in the [foundations](ch-persistence.html#sec-foundations-attractor) and [network model](ch-memory-dynamics.html#sec-memory-spikes) stores horizontal eye position. Noise moves the stored value along that attractor.[^p2-pathway] [The signal reaches [**ocular motoneurons (OMNs)**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}, neurons whose spikes activate the eye muscles.]{.definition-explanation} [The recordings came from the [**abducens nucleus**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}, a group of brainstem neurons that includes OMNs activating the lateral rectus muscle, which turns the eye outward.]{.definition-explanation} Other neurons in that nucleus carry signals to other neurons rather than directly to muscle. The study separated these cell types by how their firing changed with eye position and movement. [Finally, the muscles and the mechanical properties of the eye, together called the [**ocular plant**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}, turn neural activity into movement.]{.definition-explanation}[^p2-recordings]
Original paper figure: Ben-Shushan et al. (2022), Extended Data Figure 6
{{block:fig:PAPER-EYE-ED6}}
There are three possible contributions to an observed drift: - A changing shared command sent to many OMNs. - Private spike variability in individual OMNs. - Variability after those neurons, including muscle and measurement noise. [Private spike fluctuations can partly cancel when many neurons act together. A common command survives this averaging.]{.key-statement} This is why the noisy activity of one neuron can reveal a source that dominates the much smoother eye movement. ## The recordings pair one motor neuron with movement at a time {#sec:EYE-RECORDINGS} The authors reanalyzed earlier experiments in two male rhesus macaques. With their heads held still, the monkeys first looked at a stationary spot of light on a monitor and then followed the moving spot. A wire search coil on one eye measured the eye's angle while an electrode recorded one neuron's spikes. There were 57 identified OMNs. [Each recording paired one OMN with eye movement. There were no simultaneous recordings of multiple OMNs. Thus the analysis cannot directly measure the covariance between two recorded motor neurons.]{.key-statement}[^p2-recordings][^p2-single] The initial stationary target was followed by 500–700 ms of required fixation before the target stepped and began moving. Neural voltage was sampled at 25 kHz and eye position at 1 kHz. The authors detected microsaccades using eye speed and acceleration, removed 30 ms on each side of them, and manually checked the remaining segments. For the main displacement analysis, segments shorter than 350 ms were excluded and longer ones were split into nonoverlapping 350 ms pieces. There were 302 such pieces per cell on average, with different counts across cells. These repeated observations improve estimates within two animals. They do not create 57 independent animal samples.[^p2-segments]
Original paper figure: Ben-Shushan et al. (2022), Extended Data Figure 7
{{block:fig:PAPER-EYE-ED7}}
The large movements have a useful role even though the scientific question concerns tiny drifts. They produce enough rate change to estimate how each cell's activity depends on eye movement. The fitted relationship is then applied during fixation. This transfer is an assumption to examine, because an incorrect gain during drift would change the inferred common variance. Gain is the scale that converts a change in one signal into a change in the other.
{{block:fig:EYE-PHYSICAL-AND-RECORDED}}
## A fitted model links movement to firing rate {#sec:EYE-FORWARD-FIT} Position alone does not predict a motor neuron's activity during a movement. At the same position, firing can differ when the eye is moving or accelerating. The paper therefore fits $$ \widehat f(t)=k[E(t+\Delta t)-E_T] +r\dot E(t+\Delta t)+m\ddot E(t+\Delta t). $$ Here $E$ is horizontal eye position in degrees and $\widehat f$ is predicted firing rate in spikes/s. The position threshold $E_T$ sets where the position term reaches zero. The coefficients have units $$ [k]=\frac{\text{spikes}}{\text{s}\,\text{deg}},\qquad [r]=\frac{\text{spikes}}{\text{deg}},\qquad [m]=\frac{\text{spikes}\,\text{s}}{\text{deg}}. $$ Multiplying by position, velocity, and acceleration gives spikes/s in all three terms. The position term describes ongoing firing associated with holding the eye at an angle. The velocity term allows a different rate while the eye passes through that same angle. The acceleration term allows another change while its velocity changes. Thus $k$, $r$, and $m$ describe different demands on the motor signal. They are fitted coefficients of the combined neural and mechanical relationship. In particular, $m$ is not a direct measurement of the eye's mass. The delay $\Delta t$ is in seconds: firing at time $t$ predicts movement at the later time $t+\Delta t$ for a positive neural lead. This is the paper's Eq. 2, including its threshold and time shift.[^p2-forward] The observed rate $f(t)$ was estimated as the inverse of the interval between successive spikes, constant between those spikes. For each cell, the authors minimized the sum of squared rate errors, $$ L=\sum_{a=1}^{n_{\rm trials}}\sum_{t_j\in[0,T_a]} \left[f_a(t_j)-\widehat f_a(t_j;k,r,m,\Delta t,E_T)\right]^2. $$ $a$ labels trials and $T_a$ is trial duration. This is Eq. 3 with the trial count renamed so that it cannot be confused with a neuron count. Fits used full trials, including fixation and pursuit. To predict a trial's rate, that trial was left out of the parameter fit. Acceleration was estimated from velocity after local polynomial smoothing over 21 ms. Trials in which the rate fell below 20 Hz were discarded: the linear formula is intended for active cells above firing threshold, whereas firing cannot become negative.[^p2-forward] During fixation, the authors subtracted each segment's mean firing rate, joined the segments, and compared observed and predicted rate fluctuations. Figure 1c illustrates a weak relationship for one cell. Fig. 1d shows a positive population effect. The one sided test asks whether the mean correlation is positive, compared with a zero-mean reference. [Its [**p value**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} is the probability, under that reference, of a test statistic at least as large as observed.]{.definition-explanation} Across 57 cells it gave $p=3\times10^{-9}$. A weak single cell relationship is expected here because the tiny movement produces small rate changes against much larger spike variability. This is the first evidence of a relationship, before any estimate of the fraction of common motion.[^p2-rate-result]
Original paper figure: Ben-Shushan et al. (2022), Figure 1
{{block:fig:PAPER-EYE-1}}
## A calibrated filter predicts eye position from one cell's spikes {#sec:EYE-INVERSE-FILTER} To ask how much eye movement is shared with a neuron, it helps to express both signals in degrees. [The paper reverses the fitted relationship: a cell's spike train becomes the input, and its prediction of eye position becomes the output. This operation is an inverse of the movement-to-rate fit, rather than a new fit to small drift residuals.]{.key-statement} Let $x(t)=E(t)-E_T$. Ignoring the time shift for a moment, the deterministic relation is $$ m\ddot x+r\dot x+kx=f. $$ [A [**causal filter**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} computes its present output from present and past input. For the equation above, its [**impulse response**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} $h_0(u)$ is the position response to one instantaneous spike at time zero.]{.definition-explanation} To factor the equation, consider a time component $e^{pt}$: differentiation multiplies it by $p$. The algebraic ratio of output to input for that component is $$ H_0(p)=\frac{1}{mp^2+rp+k} =\frac{1}{m(p+1/\tau_+)(p+1/\tau_-)}. $$ Factoring the quadratic gives the slow and fast decay times $$ \tau_+=\frac{2}{r/m-\sqrt{(r/m)^2-4k/m}},\qquad \tau_-=\frac{2}{r/m+\sqrt{(r/m)^2-4k/m}}. $$ These are the paired signs in the paper's Eq. 7, with $\tau_+>\tau_-$ when $k,r,m>0$ and $r^2>4km$. Under these conditions both components decay without oscillation. At rest, the inverse equation gives $x=f/k$: with the threshold fixed, doubling $k$ halves the position offset predicted from the same steady firing rate. During a change, $r$ and $m$ also affect the response through the two timescales. This is a consequence of the fitted relationship, not evidence that changing one recorded neuron's rate alone sets eye position. The same factorization gives two useful identities: $$ \tau_+\tau_-=\frac{m}{k},\qquad \tau_++\tau_-=\frac{r}{k}. $$ The corresponding impulse response is $$ h_0(u)=\frac{\Theta(u)}{m}\, \frac{\tau_+\tau_-}{\tau_+-\tau_-} \left(e^{-u/\tau_+}-e^{-u/\tau_-}\right). $$ $\Theta(u)$ is zero for $u<0$ and one for $u>0$, which makes the response zero before the input. Restoring the fitted neural lead delays this response: $h(u)=h_0(u-\Delta t)$. Write the spike train as $\xi(t)=\sum_j\delta(t-t_j)$, where $\delta$ is an ideal instantaneous impulse of unit area, so integration over one spike counts one event. The prediction is $$ \widehat E(t)=E_T+\int_{-\infty}^{t}h(t-v)\xi(v)\,dv =E_T+\sum_j h(t-t_j). $$ These expressions reproduce Eqs. 4–6, including the factor $\tau_+\tau_-/m$ and the delay. [The [**convolution**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} integral adds the responses to all past spikes.]{.definition-explanation} With spike count treated as a count, $\xi$ has units spikes/s and $h$ has units degrees/spike. Each spike contributes a decaying position response. Adding those responses produces degrees.[^p2-inversion] ::: {.publisher-clarification-note .publisher-fold-always title="Derivation: the weights of the two decaying responses"} We can obtain the response to a spike directly from the differential equation. After the spike, the input is zero, and each of the two exponentials solves the remaining homogeneous equation. Write their combination as $$ h_0(u)=A e^{-u/\tau_+}+B e^{-u/\tau_-},\qquad u>0. $$ To find $A$ and $B$, treat the spike as a short pulse of unit area and shrink its duration to zero. The position change during that pulse tends to zero, so $h_0(0^+)=0$. Integrating $m h_0''+r h_0'+k h_0$ across the pulse gives $m h_0'(0^+)=1$: the velocity changes by $1/m$, while position and velocity before the causal response are zero. Therefore $$ A+B=0,\qquad -\frac{A}{\tau_+}-\frac{B}{\tau_-}=\frac1m. $$ Substituting $B=-A$ gives $A(1/\tau_- -1/\tau_+)=1/m$, hence $A=\tau_+\tau_-/[m(\tau_+-\tau_-)]$. Making the response zero before the spike gives the impulse response $h_0(u)$. ::: For a constructed example, take $k=4$ spikes/(s deg), $\tau_+=0.120$ s, and $\tau_-=0.005$ s. The identities above require $r=0.500$ spikes/deg and $m=0.00240$ spikes s/deg. Then $$ h_0(u)=2.174\left(e^{-u/0.120}-e^{-u/0.005}\right) \ \text{deg/spike},\quad u>0, $$ and its area is $2.174(0.120-0.005)=0.250$ deg s/spike, equal to $1/k$. A steady rate of 80 spikes/s predicts an offset of 20 degrees above $E_T$. This checks the gain and the time constants. ::: {.publisher-clarification-note .publisher-fold-always title="Check: static gain and equal decay times"} The kernel's area checks its normalization: $$ \int_0^\infty h_0(u)\,du =\frac{\tau_+\tau_-}{m(\tau_+-\tau_-)}(\tau_+-\tau_-) =\frac1k. $$ Thus a constant input rate $f_0$ predicts $E_T+f_0/k$, exactly the static forward relation. A kernel with unit area would give the wrong conversion unless $k$ had already been absorbed into the input. When the two decay times coincide, $r^2=4km$, the limit is $h_0(u)=\Theta(u)u e^{-u/\tau}/m$. The distinct exponential formula is used for the fitted responses in the paper. ::: Figure 2a–b shows typical fitted times of about 5 ms and 120 ms. Figure 2c shows that a single cell's reconstructed drift is much noisier than the measured movement. Across 350 ms displacement pairs, the mean Pearson correlation was $\langle R\rangle=0.17\pm0.02$, [where the error is the [**standard error of the mean (SEM)**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}. SEM estimates uncertainty in the across-cell mean, rather than the spread of individual cells or uncertainty across animals.]{.definition-explanation} The one sided test gave $p=3.8\times10^{-12}$. Shuffling which measured segment was paired with which spike prediction centered the comparison near zero. Here and below $\langle\cdot\rangle$ over cells means a population average.[^p2-correlation]
Original paper figure: Ben-Shushan et al. (2022), Figure 2
{{block:fig:PAPER-EYE-2}}
## The measured correlation challenges independent motor noise alone {#sec:EYE-SHARED-VARIANCE} A correlation of 0.17 does not immediately tell us how much motion comes from the common command. First we can ask a more limited question: could all the motion come from independent motor neuron fluctuations? For a centered displacement $Y$ and one centered prediction $X$, the best linear prediction $bX$ minimizes $\operatorname{Var}(Y-bX)$. Differentiating with respect to $b$ gives $b=\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)/\operatorname{Var}(X)$. Its explained fraction of variance is $$ \frac{b^2\operatorname{Var}(X)}{\operatorname{Var}(Y)} =\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)^2}{\operatorname{Var}(X)\operatorname{Var}(Y)} =R^2. $$ [This is the [**coefficient of determination**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} for a linear prediction with a fitted gain.]{.definition-explanation} It does not assert that the raw, unscaled position predictor itself has a small squared error. Suppose there are $N_m$ independent single neuron predictors $X_i$. Standardize each to variance one and also standardize $Y$. Independence makes the $X_i$ uncorrelated, so the residual after using them all has variance $$ \operatorname{Var}\left(Y-\sum_i R_iX_i\right) =1-2\sum_iR_i^2+\sum_iR_i^2 =1-\sum_iR_i^2\ge0. $$ Consequently $\sum_iR_i^2\le1$, and an average neuron explains at most $1/N_m$. This proves the bound used in Supplementary Eq. S1. It does not require equal muscle effects from all neurons. Applying it to the sampled cells does require their average explanatory power to represent the relevant motor population.[^p2-independent-bound] The authors avoid directly averaging noisy squared correlations. Instead, $$ \langle R^2\rangle-\langle R\rangle^2=\operatorname{Var}(R)\ge0, \qquad \langle R^2\rangle\ge(0.17)^2=0.0289. $$ [Thus the estimated mean correlation implies an average explained fraction of at least about 2.9%. For 1,000 independently contributing motor neurons, the bound would be 0.1%. For several thousand it is smaller. The mismatch argues against independent OMN noise as the sole source.]{.key-statement} Shared fluctuations can allow many cells to explain the same part of the movement, so their explained fractions can overlap.[^p2-independent-bound] This step finds shared variation. Locating its source upstream also uses a biological premise: the private variability generated within OMNs is taken to be independent across cells. The paper supports that premise using anatomical and stimulation studies indicating little local recurrent coupling in the relevant motor nuclei. It was not tested by simultaneous recordings in this data set. Common inputs can correlate the total activity of OMNs even when their privately generated spike noise is independent.[^p2-independence] ## Calibrated covariance estimates the common share of movement variance {#sec:EYE-CHI} The variance bound establishes that a shared signal exists, but leaves its size open. The next calculation uses the inverse filter’s calibrated gain in degrees. For one 350 ms interval, write the measured displacement and the single cell prediction as $$ Y=\delta E=C+\eta,\qquad X=\delta\widehat E=C+\epsilon, $$ where $C=\delta E_C$ is the common upstream contribution, $\eta$ combines motor neuron, muscle, and measurement contributions to measured displacement, and $\epsilon$ is the prediction error from the individual cell. All are displacement variables in degrees. The calculation assumes: - The common contribution enters both signals with unit gain, meaning the same one-for-one displacement scale. - $C,\eta,\epsilon$ are pairwise uncorrelated to the required accuracy. Expanding the covariance shows why those assumptions matter: $$ \operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=\operatorname{Var}(C) +\operatorname{Cov}(C,\eta)+\operatorname{Cov}(\epsilon,C) +\operatorname{Cov}(\epsilon,\eta) \simeq\operatorname{Var}(C). $$ The common fraction is therefore estimated by $$ \chi=\frac{\operatorname{Var}(C)}{\operatorname{Var}(Y)} \simeq\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)}{\operatorname{Var}(Y)}. $$ These are Eqs. 11–15 in displacement form. The gain assumption requires that the relation calibrated during larger movements still applies during drift. There is also a small covariance between $\epsilon$ and $\eta$, because the recorded neuron's private spikes contribute both to its predictor and to actual eye motion. The paper neglects this contribution as order $1/N_m$ under its many neuron model.[^p2-chi-method] Correlation divides the same covariance by a different denominator: $$ R=\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)}{\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(X)\operatorname{Var}(Y)}}, \qquad \chi\simeq R\sqrt{\frac{\operatorname{Var}(X)}{\operatorname{Var}(Y)}}. $$ [Large private noise in a cell inflates $\operatorname{Var}(X)$ and makes $R$ small. It need not make the common contribution to the real movement small, because many independent private contributions average down there.]{.key-statement}
**Example: correlation 0.17 with a common fraction 0.82.** These numbers are constructed to expose the distinction, not extracted from individual cells. Take independent centered variables with $$ \operatorname{Var}(C)=0.00820\ \text{deg}^2,\quad \operatorname{Var}(\eta)=0.00180\ \text{deg}^2,\quad \operatorname{Var}(\epsilon)=0.22446\ \text{deg}^2. $$ Then $\operatorname{Var}(Y)=0.01000$, $\operatorname{Var}(X)=0.23266$, and $\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=0.00820$, all in deg$^2$. It follows that $$ R=\frac{0.00820}{\sqrt{0.01000\times0.23266}}\simeq0.170, \qquad \chi=\frac{0.00820}{0.01000}=0.820. $$ One cell explains $R^2\simeq2.89\%$ of displacement variance after linear rescaling, while the common signal supplies 82% of actual displacement variance. The larger, poorly predicted part of the single cell signal is private prediction noise.
{{block:fig:EYE-SHARED-PRIVATE-VARIANCE}}
The bars use the same physical scale, so the equal common pieces have equal lengths. See [Shared and private variability, Eqs. 11–15, p. 10](../papers/ben-shushan-2022-fixational-drift.pdf#page=10).
In the experiment, each cell gives a noisy estimate $\chi_i$, and those estimates can lie outside $[0,1]$. The underlying variance fraction remains in that interval under the model, but the sample covariance need not. The paper estimates each standard error $\Delta\chi_i$ mainly from covariance uncertainty, treating the measured displacement variance in the denominator as comparatively well determined. It then uses inverse variance weighting: $$ w_i=\frac{1}{(\Delta\chi_i)^2},\qquad \widehat\chi=\frac{\sum_iw_i\chi_i}{\sum_iw_i},\qquad \sigma_{\widehat\chi}=\left(\sum_iw_i\right)^{-1/2}. $$ To see the weighting, let normalized weights $a_i$ sum to one. Independent errors give variance $\sum_i a_i^2(\Delta\chi_i)^2$ for $\sum_i a_i\chi_i$. Minimizing this subject to $\sum_i a_i=1$ gives $a_i\propto1/(\Delta\chi_i)^2$ and the error above. The paper additionally assumes approximately normal errors around a common value. The last expression is a propagated estimation error under those assumptions. It does not measure variation across animals or uncertainty in the gain and independence assumptions. It is neither a fraction of distance traveled nor the fraction that one neuron's spikes accurately predict.]{.key-statement}[^p2-chi-error] [^p2-question]: Ben-Shushan, N., Shaham, N., Joshua, M., & Burak, Y. With their heads held still, the monkeys first looked at a stationary spot of light on a monitor and then followed the moving spot. A wire search coil on one eye measured the eye's angle while an electrode recorded one neuron's spikes. There were 57 identified OMNs. [Each recording paired one OMN with eye movement. For the main displacement analysis, segments shorter than 350 ms were excluded and longer ones were split into nonoverlapping 350 ms pieces. There were 302 such pieces per cell on average, with different counts across cells. These repeated observations improve estimates within two animals. They do not create 57 independent animal samples.[^p2-segments]

review_metadata.title: Eye drift points to a shared neural drive
review_metadata.purpose: Even when a monkey looks at a stationary spot, its eyes drift slightly. This chapter explains how paired measurements of eye angle and the firing of neurons that command eye muscles support a shared neural source of that drift, before considering a particular circuit mechanism.

section_list.title: From stored eye position to muscle action
section_list.summary: The eye needs an ongoing command to maintain a position. A brief command to move is therefore insufficient: after the movement, a circuit must maintain activity representing the new position. The [**oculomotor integrator**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} is the neural circuit that performs this storage. “Integrator” refers to turning a movement command into a lasting position signal. In the proposed mechanism, the continuous attractor described in the [foundations](ch-persistence.html#sec-foundations-attractor) and [network model](ch-memory-dynamics.html#sec-memory-spikes) stores horizontal eye position. Noise moves the stored value along that attractor.[^p2-pathway]
