# Eye drift points to a shared neural drive {#ch:EYE-DRIFT} Looking steadily at a small spot does not hold the eye perfectly still. [Between brief, rapid movements called [**microsaccades**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}, the eye makes a small, smooth, irregular movement called fixational drift.]{.definition-explanation} [Does this movement begin as noise in the muscles, or does the brain send a changing command to them?]{.key-statement} Ben-Shushan and colleagues answer this in two stages. Their recordings support a large shared drive upstream of the motor neurons. Their model then proposes a particular source: random motion of the eye position stored in a memory circuit.[^p2-question] This distinction connects the previous chapters to a measurement outside the brain. A memory coordinate can diffuse inside a neural network, but the movement produced by that coordinate also depends on the muscles and the mechanics of the eye. We need to follow the signal through those stages before comparing a neural diffusion law with an eye trajectory. A recording from one motor neuron becomes useful for this comparison only after its spikes and the eye's movement can be expressed on the same scale. The larger movements provide that calibration. Applying it during fixation then lets us ask whether independent motor noise could explain the observed relationship, and estimate the shared contribution under explicit gain and independence assumptions. ## From stored eye position to muscle action {#sec:EYE-PATHWAY} The eye needs an ongoing command to maintain a position. A brief command to move is therefore insufficient: after the movement, a circuit must maintain activity representing the new position. [The [**oculomotor integrator**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} is the neural circuit that performs this storage. “Integrator” refers to turning a movement command into a lasting position signal.]{.definition-explanation} In the proposed mechanism, the continuous attractor described in the [foundations](ch-persistence.html#sec-foundations-attractor) and [network model](ch-memory-dynamics.html#sec-memory-spikes) stores horizontal eye position. Noise moves the stored value along that attractor.[^p2-pathway] [The signal reaches [**ocular motoneurons (OMNs)**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}, neurons whose spikes activate the eye muscles.]{.definition-explanation} [The recordings came from the [**abducens nucleus**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}, a group of brainstem neurons that includes OMNs activating the lateral rectus muscle, which turns the eye outward.]{.definition-explanation} Other neurons in that nucleus carry signals to other neurons rather than directly to muscle. The study separated these cell types by how their firing changed with eye position and movement. [Finally, the muscles and the mechanical properties of the eye, together called the [**ocular plant**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}, turn neural activity into movement.]{.definition-explanation}[^p2-recordings]
Original paper figure: Ben-Shushan et al. (2022), Extended Data Figure 6
{{block:fig:PAPER-EYE-ED6}}
There are three possible contributions to an observed drift: - A changing shared command sent to many OMNs. - Private spike variability in individual OMNs. - Variability after those neurons, including muscle and measurement noise. [Private spike fluctuations can partly cancel when many neurons act together. A common command survives this averaging.]{.key-statement} This is why the noisy activity of one neuron can reveal a source that dominates the much smoother eye movement. ## The recordings pair one motor neuron with movement at a time {#sec:EYE-RECORDINGS} The authors reanalyzed earlier experiments in two male rhesus macaques. With their heads held still, the monkeys first looked at a stationary spot of light on a monitor and then followed the moving spot. A wire search coil on one eye measured the eye's angle while an electrode recorded one neuron's spikes. There were 57 identified OMNs. [Each recording paired one OMN with eye movement. There were no simultaneous recordings of multiple OMNs. Thus the analysis cannot directly measure the covariance between two recorded motor neurons.]{.key-statement}[^p2-recordings][^p2-single] The initial stationary target was followed by 500–700 ms of required fixation before the target stepped and began moving. Neural voltage was sampled at 25 kHz and eye position at 1 kHz. The authors detected microsaccades using eye speed and acceleration, removed 30 ms on each side of them, and manually checked the remaining segments. For the main displacement analysis, segments shorter than 350 ms were excluded and longer ones were split into nonoverlapping 350 ms pieces. There were 302 such pieces per cell on average, with different counts across cells. These repeated observations improve estimates within two animals. They do not create 57 independent animal samples.[^p2-segments]
Original paper figure: Ben-Shushan et al. (2022), Extended Data Figure 7
{{block:fig:PAPER-EYE-ED7}}
The large movements have a useful role even though the scientific question concerns tiny drifts. They produce enough rate change to estimate how each cell's activity depends on eye movement. The fitted relationship is then applied during fixation. This transfer is an assumption to examine, because an incorrect gain during drift would change the inferred common variance. Gain is the scale that converts a change in one signal into a change in the other.
{{block:fig:EYE-PHYSICAL-AND-RECORDED}}
## A fitted model links movement to firing rate {#sec:EYE-FORWARD-FIT} Position alone does not predict a motor neuron's activity during a movement. At the same position, firing can differ when the eye is moving or accelerating. The paper therefore fits $$ \widehat f(t)=k[E(t+\Delta t)-E_T] +r\dot E(t+\Delta t)+m\ddot E(t+\Delta t). $$ Here $E$ is horizontal eye position in degrees and $\widehat f$ is predicted firing rate in spikes/s. The position threshold $E_T$ sets where the position term reaches zero. The coefficients have units $$ [k]=\frac{\text{spikes}}{\text{s}\,\text{deg}},\qquad [r]=\frac{\text{spikes}}{\text{deg}},\qquad [m]=\frac{\text{spikes}\,\text{s}}{\text{deg}}. $$ Multiplying by position, velocity, and acceleration gives spikes/s in all three terms. The position term describes ongoing firing associated with holding the eye at an angle. The velocity term allows a different rate while the eye passes through that same angle. The acceleration term allows another change while its velocity changes. Thus $k$, $r$, and $m$ describe different demands on the motor signal. They are fitted coefficients of the combined neural and mechanical relationship. In particular, $m$ is not a direct measurement of the eye's mass. The delay $\Delta t$ is in seconds: firing at time $t$ predicts movement at the later time $t+\Delta t$ for a positive neural lead. This is the paper's Eq. 2, including its threshold and time shift.[^p2-forward] The observed rate $f(t)$ was estimated as the inverse of the interval between successive spikes, constant between those spikes. For each cell, the authors minimized the sum of squared rate errors, $$ L=\sum_{a=1}^{n_{\rm trials}}\sum_{t_j\in[0,T_a]} \left[f_a(t_j)-\widehat f_a(t_j;k,r,m,\Delta t,E_T)\right]^2. $$ $a$ labels trials and $T_a$ is trial duration. This is Eq. 3 with the trial count renamed so that it cannot be confused with a neuron count. Fits used full trials, including fixation and pursuit. To predict a trial's rate, that trial was left out of the parameter fit. Acceleration was estimated from velocity after local polynomial smoothing over 21 ms. Trials in which the rate fell below 20 Hz were discarded: the linear formula is intended for active cells above firing threshold, whereas firing cannot become negative.[^p2-forward] During fixation, the authors subtracted each segment's mean firing rate, joined the segments, and compared observed and predicted rate fluctuations. Figure 1c illustrates a weak relationship for one cell. Fig. 1d shows a positive population effect. The one sided test asks whether the mean correlation is positive, compared with a zero-mean reference. [Its [**p value**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} is the probability, under that reference, of a test statistic at least as large as observed.]{.definition-explanation} Across 57 cells it gave $p=3\times10^{-9}$. A weak single cell relationship is expected here because the tiny movement produces small rate changes against much larger spike variability. This is the first evidence of a relationship, before any estimate of the fraction of common motion.[^p2-rate-result]
Original paper figure: Ben-Shushan et al. (2022), Figure 1
{{block:fig:PAPER-EYE-1}}
## A calibrated filter predicts eye position from one cell's spikes {#sec:EYE-INVERSE-FILTER} To ask how much eye movement is shared with a neuron, it helps to express both signals in degrees. [The paper reverses the fitted relationship: a cell's spike train becomes the input, and its prediction of eye position becomes the output. This operation is an inverse of the movement-to-rate fit, rather than a new fit to small drift residuals.]{.key-statement} Let $x(t)=E(t)-E_T$. Ignoring the time shift for a moment, the deterministic relation is $$ m\ddot x+r\dot x+kx=f. $$ [A [**causal filter**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} computes its present output from present and past input. For the equation above, its [**impulse response**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} $h_0(u)$ is the position response to one instantaneous spike at time zero.]{.definition-explanation} To factor the equation, consider a time component $e^{pt}$: differentiation multiplies it by $p$. The algebraic ratio of output to input for that component is $$ H_0(p)=\frac{1}{mp^2+rp+k} =\frac{1}{m(p+1/\tau_+)(p+1/\tau_-)}. $$ Factoring the quadratic gives the slow and fast decay times $$ \tau_+=\frac{2}{r/m-\sqrt{(r/m)^2-4k/m}},\qquad \tau_-=\frac{2}{r/m+\sqrt{(r/m)^2-4k/m}}. $$ These are the paired signs in the paper's Eq. 7, with $\tau_+>\tau_-$ when $k,r,m>0$ and $r^2>4km$. Under these conditions both components decay without oscillation. At rest, the inverse equation gives $x=f/k$: with the threshold fixed, doubling $k$ halves the position offset predicted from the same steady firing rate. During a change, $r$ and $m$ also affect the response through the two timescales. This is a consequence of the fitted relationship, not evidence that changing one recorded neuron's rate alone sets eye position. The same factorization gives two useful identities: $$ \tau_+\tau_-=\frac{m}{k},\qquad \tau_++\tau_-=\frac{r}{k}. $$ The corresponding impulse response is $$ h_0(u)=\frac{\Theta(u)}{m}\, \frac{\tau_+\tau_-}{\tau_+-\tau_-} \left(e^{-u/\tau_+}-e^{-u/\tau_-}\right). $$ $\Theta(u)$ is zero for $u<0$ and one for $u>0$, which makes the response zero before the input. Restoring the fitted neural lead delays this response: $h(u)=h_0(u-\Delta t)$. Write the spike train as $\xi(t)=\sum_j\delta(t-t_j)$, where $\delta$ is an ideal instantaneous impulse of unit area, so integration over one spike counts one event. The prediction is $$ \widehat E(t)=E_T+\int_{-\infty}^{t}h(t-v)\xi(v)\,dv =E_T+\sum_j h(t-t_j). $$ These expressions reproduce Eqs. 4–6, including the factor $\tau_+\tau_-/m$ and the delay. [The [**convolution**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} integral adds the responses to all past spikes.]{.definition-explanation} With spike count treated as a count, $\xi$ has units spikes/s and $h$ has units degrees/spike. Each spike contributes a decaying position response. Adding those responses produces degrees.[^p2-inversion] ::: {.publisher-clarification-note .publisher-fold-always title="Derivation: the weights of the two decaying responses"} We can obtain the response to a spike directly from the differential equation. After the spike, the input is zero, and each of the two exponentials solves the remaining homogeneous equation. Write their combination as $$ h_0(u)=A e^{-u/\tau_+}+B e^{-u/\tau_-},\qquad u>0. $$ To find $A$ and $B$, treat the spike as a short pulse of unit area and shrink its duration to zero. The position change during that pulse tends to zero, so $h_0(0^+)=0$. Integrating $m h_0''+r h_0'+k h_0$ across the pulse gives $m h_0'(0^+)=1$: the velocity changes by $1/m$, while position and velocity before the causal response are zero. Therefore $$ A+B=0,\qquad -\frac{A}{\tau_+}-\frac{B}{\tau_-}=\frac1m. $$ Substituting $B=-A$ gives $A(1/\tau_- -1/\tau_+)=1/m$, hence $A=\tau_+\tau_-/[m(\tau_+-\tau_-)]$. Making the response zero before the spike gives the impulse response $h_0(u)$. ::: For a constructed example, take $k=4$ spikes/(s deg), $\tau_+=0.120$ s, and $\tau_-=0.005$ s. The identities above require $r=0.500$ spikes/deg and $m=0.00240$ spikes s/deg. Then $$ h_0(u)=2.174\left(e^{-u/0.120}-e^{-u/0.005}\right) \ \text{deg/spike},\quad u>0, $$ and its area is $2.174(0.120-0.005)=0.250$ deg s/spike, equal to $1/k$. A steady rate of 80 spikes/s predicts an offset of 20 degrees above $E_T$. This checks the gain and the time constants. ::: {.publisher-clarification-note .publisher-fold-always title="Check: static gain and equal decay times"} The kernel's area checks its normalization: $$ \int_0^\infty h_0(u)\,du =\frac{\tau_+\tau_-}{m(\tau_+-\tau_-)}(\tau_+-\tau_-) =\frac1k. $$ Thus a constant input rate $f_0$ predicts $E_T+f_0/k$, exactly the static forward relation. A kernel with unit area would give the wrong conversion unless $k$ had already been absorbed into the input. When the two decay times coincide, $r^2=4km$, the limit is $h_0(u)=\Theta(u)u e^{-u/\tau}/m$. The distinct exponential formula is used for the fitted responses in the paper. ::: Figure 2a–b shows typical fitted times of about 5 ms and 120 ms. Figure 2c shows that a single cell's reconstructed drift is much noisier than the measured movement. Across 350 ms displacement pairs, the mean Pearson correlation was $\langle R\rangle=0.17\pm0.02$, [where the error is the [**standard error of the mean (SEM)**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}. SEM estimates uncertainty in the across-cell mean, rather than the spread of individual cells or uncertainty across animals.]{.definition-explanation} The one sided test gave $p=3.8\times10^{-12}$. Shuffling which measured segment was paired with which spike prediction centered the comparison near zero. Here and below $\langle\cdot\rangle$ over cells means a population average.[^p2-correlation]
Original paper figure: Ben-Shushan et al. (2022), Figure 2
{{block:fig:PAPER-EYE-2}}
## The measured correlation challenges independent motor noise alone {#sec:EYE-SHARED-VARIANCE} A correlation of 0.17 does not immediately tell us how much motion comes from the common command. First we can ask a more limited question: could all the motion come from independent motor neuron fluctuations? For a centered displacement $Y$ and one centered prediction $X$, the best linear prediction $bX$ minimizes $\operatorname{Var}(Y-bX)$. Differentiating with respect to $b$ gives $b=\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)/\operatorname{Var}(X)$. Its explained fraction of variance is $$ \frac{b^2\operatorname{Var}(X)}{\operatorname{Var}(Y)} =\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)^2}{\operatorname{Var}(X)\operatorname{Var}(Y)} =R^2. $$ [This is the [**coefficient of determination**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} for a linear prediction with a fitted gain.]{.definition-explanation} It does not assert that the raw, unscaled position predictor itself has a small squared error. Suppose there are $N_m$ independent single neuron predictors $X_i$. Standardize each to variance one and also standardize $Y$. Independence makes the $X_i$ uncorrelated, so the residual after using them all has variance $$ \operatorname{Var}\left(Y-\sum_i R_iX_i\right) =1-2\sum_iR_i^2+\sum_iR_i^2 =1-\sum_iR_i^2\ge0. $$ Consequently $\sum_iR_i^2\le1$, and an average neuron explains at most $1/N_m$. This proves the bound used in Supplementary Eq. S1. It does not require equal muscle effects from all neurons. Applying it to the sampled cells does require their average explanatory power to represent the relevant motor population.[^p2-independent-bound] The authors avoid directly averaging noisy squared correlations. Instead, $$ \langle R^2\rangle-\langle R\rangle^2=\operatorname{Var}(R)\ge0, \qquad \langle R^2\rangle\ge(0.17)^2=0.0289. $$ [Thus the estimated mean correlation implies an average explained fraction of at least about 2.9%. For 1,000 independently contributing motor neurons, the bound would be 0.1%. For several thousand it is smaller. The mismatch argues against independent OMN noise as the sole source.]{.key-statement} Shared fluctuations can allow many cells to explain the same part of the movement, so their explained fractions can overlap.[^p2-independent-bound] This step finds shared variation. Locating its source upstream also uses a biological premise: the private variability generated within OMNs is taken to be independent across cells. The paper supports that premise using anatomical and stimulation studies indicating little local recurrent coupling in the relevant motor nuclei. It was not tested by simultaneous recordings in this data set. Common inputs can correlate the total activity of OMNs even when their privately generated spike noise is independent.[^p2-independence] ## Calibrated covariance estimates the common share of movement variance {#sec:EYE-CHI} The variance bound establishes that a shared signal exists, but leaves its size open. The next calculation uses the inverse filter’s calibrated gain in degrees. For one 350 ms interval, write the measured displacement and the single cell prediction as $$ Y=\delta E=C+\eta,\qquad X=\delta\widehat E=C+\epsilon, $$ where $C=\delta E_C$ is the common upstream contribution, $\eta$ combines motor neuron, muscle, and measurement contributions to measured displacement, and $\epsilon$ is the prediction error from the individual cell. All are displacement variables in degrees. The calculation assumes: - The common contribution enters both signals with unit gain, meaning the same one-for-one displacement scale. - $C,\eta,\epsilon$ are pairwise uncorrelated to the required accuracy. Expanding the covariance shows why those assumptions matter: $$ \operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=\operatorname{Var}(C) +\operatorname{Cov}(C,\eta)+\operatorname{Cov}(\epsilon,C) +\operatorname{Cov}(\epsilon,\eta) \simeq\operatorname{Var}(C). $$ The common fraction is therefore estimated by $$ \chi=\frac{\operatorname{Var}(C)}{\operatorname{Var}(Y)} \simeq\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)}{\operatorname{Var}(Y)}. $$ These are Eqs. 11–15 in displacement form. The gain assumption requires that the relation calibrated during larger movements still applies during drift. There is also a small covariance between $\epsilon$ and $\eta$, because the recorded neuron's private spikes contribute both to its predictor and to actual eye motion. The paper neglects this contribution as order $1/N_m$ under its many neuron model.[^p2-chi-method] Correlation divides the same covariance by a different denominator: $$ R=\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)}{\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(X)\operatorname{Var}(Y)}}, \qquad \chi\simeq R\sqrt{\frac{\operatorname{Var}(X)}{\operatorname{Var}(Y)}}. $$ [Large private noise in a cell inflates $\operatorname{Var}(X)$ and makes $R$ small. It need not make the common contribution to the real movement small, because many independent private contributions average down there.]{.key-statement}
**Example: correlation 0.17 with a common fraction 0.82.** These numbers are constructed to expose the distinction, not extracted from individual cells. Take independent centered variables with $$ \operatorname{Var}(C)=0.00820\ \text{deg}^2,\quad \operatorname{Var}(\eta)=0.00180\ \text{deg}^2,\quad \operatorname{Var}(\epsilon)=0.22446\ \text{deg}^2. $$ Then $\operatorname{Var}(Y)=0.01000$, $\operatorname{Var}(X)=0.23266$, and $\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=0.00820$, all in deg$^2$. It follows that $$ R=\frac{0.00820}{\sqrt{0.01000\times0.23266}}\simeq0.170, \qquad \chi=\frac{0.00820}{0.01000}=0.820. $$ One cell explains $R^2\simeq2.89\%$ of displacement variance after linear rescaling, while the common signal supplies 82% of actual displacement variance. The larger, poorly predicted part of the single cell signal is private prediction noise.
{{block:fig:EYE-SHARED-PRIVATE-VARIANCE}}
The bars use the same physical scale, so the equal common pieces have equal lengths. See [Shared and private variability, Eqs. 11–15, p. 10](../papers/ben-shushan-2022-fixational-drift.pdf#page=10).
In the experiment, each cell gives a noisy estimate $\chi_i$, and those estimates can lie outside $[0,1]$. The underlying variance fraction remains in that interval under the model, but the sample covariance need not. The paper estimates each standard error $\Delta\chi_i$ mainly from covariance uncertainty, treating the measured displacement variance in the denominator as comparatively well determined. It then uses inverse variance weighting: $$ w_i=\frac{1}{(\Delta\chi_i)^2},\qquad \widehat\chi=\frac{\sum_iw_i\chi_i}{\sum_iw_i},\qquad \sigma_{\widehat\chi}=\left(\sum_iw_i\right)^{-1/2}. $$ To see the weighting, let normalized weights $a_i$ sum to one. Independent errors give variance $\sum_i a_i^2(\Delta\chi_i)^2$ for $\sum_i a_i\chi_i$. Minimizing this subject to $\sum_i a_i=1$ gives $a_i\propto1/(\Delta\chi_i)^2$ and the error above. The paper additionally assumes approximately normal errors around a common value. The last expression is a propagated estimation error under those assumptions. It does not measure variation across animals or uncertainty in the gain and independence assumptions. ## Calibrated covariance estimates the common share of movement variance {#sec:EYE-CHI} The variance bound establishes that a shared signal exists, but leaves its size open. The next calculation uses the inverse filter’s calibrated gain in degrees. For one 350 ms interval, write the measured displacement and the single cell prediction as $$ Y=\delta E=C+\eta,\qquad X=\delta\widehat E=C+\epsilon, $$ where $C=\delta E_C$ is the common upstream contribution, $\eta$ combines motor neuron, muscle, and measurement contributions to measured displacement, and $\epsilon$ is the prediction error from the individual cell. All are displacement variables in degrees. The calculation assumes: - The common contribution enters both signals with unit gain, meaning the same one-for-one displacement scale. - $C,\eta,\epsilon$ are pairwise uncorrelated to the required accuracy. Expanding the covariance shows why those assumptions matter: $$ \operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=\operatorname{Var}(C) +\operatorname{Cov}(C,\eta)+\operatorname{Cov}(\epsilon,C) +\operatorname{Cov}(\epsilon,\eta) \simeq\operatorname{Var}(C). $$ The common fraction is therefore estimated by $$ \chi=\frac{\operatorname{Var}(C)}{\operatorname{Var}(Y)} \simeq\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)}{\operatorname{Var}(Y)}. $$ These are Eqs. 11–15 in displacement form. The gain assumption requires that the relation calibrated during larger movements still applies during drift. There is also a small covariance between $\epsilon$ and $\eta$, because the recorded neuron's private spikes contribute both to its predictor and to actual eye motion. The paper neglects this contribution as order $1/N_m$ under its many neuron model.[^p2-chi-method] Correlation divides the same covariance by a different denominator: $$ R=\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)}{\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(X)\operatorname{Var}(Y)}}, \qquad \chi\simeq R\sqrt{\frac{\operatorname{Var}(X)}{\operatorname{Var}(Y)}}. $$ [Large private noise in a cell inflates $\operatorname{Var}(X)$ and makes $R$ small. It need not make the common contribution to the real movement small, because many independent private contributions average down there.]{.key-statement}
**Example: correlation 0.17 with a common fraction 0.82.** These numbers are constructed to expose the distinction, not extracted from individual cells. Take independent centered variables with $$ \operatorname{Var}(C)=0.00820\ \text{deg}^2,\quad \operatorname{Var}(\eta)=0.00180\ \text{deg}^2,\quad \operatorname{Var}(\epsilon)=0.22446\ \text{deg}^2. $$ Then $\operatorname{Var}(Y)=0.01000$, $\operatorname{Var}(X)=0.23266$, and $\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=0.00820$, all in deg$^2$. It follows that $$ R=\frac{0.00820}{\sqrt{0.01000\times0.23266}}\simeq0.170, \qquad \chi=\frac{0.00820}{0.01000}=0.820. $$ One cell explains $R^2\simeq2.89\%$ of displacement variance after linear rescaling, while the common signal supplies 82% of actual displacement variance. The larger, poorly predicted part of the single cell signal is private prediction noise.
{{block:fig:EYE-SHARED-PRIVATE-VARIANCE}}
The bars use the same physical scale, so the equal common pieces have equal lengths. See [Shared and private variability, Eqs. 11–15, p. 10](../papers/ben-shushan-2022-fixational-drift.pdf#page=10).
In the experiment, each cell gives a noisy estimate $\chi_i$, and those estimates can lie outside $[0,1]$. The underlying variance fraction remains in that interval under the model, but the sample covariance need not. The paper estimates each standard error $\Delta\chi_i$ mainly from covariance uncertainty, treating the measured displacement variance in the denominator as comparatively well determined. It then uses inverse variance weighting: $$ w_i=\frac{1}{(\Delta\chi_i)^2},\qquad \widehat\chi=\frac{\sum_iw_i\chi_i}{\sum_iw_i},\qquad \sigma_{\widehat\chi}=\left(\sum_iw_i\right)^{-1/2}. $$ To see the weighting, let normalized weights $a_i$ sum to one. Independent errors give variance $\sum_i a_i^2(\Delta\chi_i)^2$ for $\sum_i a_i\chi_i$. Minimizing this subject to $\sum_i a_i=1$ gives $a_i\propto1/(\Delta\chi_i)^2$ and the error above. The paper additionally assumes approximately normal errors around a common value. The last expression is a propagated estimation error under those assumptions. It does not measure variation across animals or uncertainty in the gain and independence assumptions. review_metadata.title: Eye drift points to a shared neural drive
review_metadata.purpose: Even when a monkey looks at a stationary spot, its eyes drift slightly. This chapter explains how paired measurements of eye angle and the firing of neurons that command eye muscles support a shared neural source of that drift, before considering a particular circuit mechanism.

section_list.title: From stored eye position to muscle action
section_list.summary: The eye needs an ongoing command to maintain a position. A brief command to move is therefore insufficient: after the movement, a circuit must maintain activity representing the new position. The [**oculomotor integrator**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} is the neural circuit that performs this storage. “Integrator” refers to turning a movement command into a lasting position signal. In the proposed mechanism, the continuous attractor described in the [foundations](ch-persistence.html#sec-foundations-attractor) and [network model](ch-memory-dynamics.html#sec-memory-spikes) stores horizontal eye position. Noise moves the stored value along that attractor.[^p2-pathway]

With their heads held still, the monkeys first looked at a stationary spot of light on a monitor and then followed the moving spot. A wire search coil on one eye measured the eye's angle while an electrode recorded one neuron's spikes. There were 57 identified OMNs. Each recording paired one OMN with eye movement. There were no simultaneous recordings of multiple OMNs. Thus the analysis cannot directly measure the covariance between two recorded motor neurons.[^p2-recordings][^p2-single]

The paper reverses the fitted relationship: a cell's spike train becomes the input, and its prediction of eye position becomes the output. # Eye drift points to a shared neural drive {#ch:EYE-DRIFT} Looking steadily at a small spot does not hold the eye perfectly still. [Between brief, rapid movements called [**microsaccades**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}, the eye makes a small, smooth, irregular movement called fixational drift.]{.definition-explanation} [Does this movement begin as noise in the muscles, or does the brain send a changing command to them?]{.key-statement} Ben-Shushan and colleagues answer this in two stages. Their recordings support a large shared drive upstream of the motor neurons. Their model then proposes a particular source: random motion of the eye position stored in a memory circuit.[^p2-question] This distinction connects the previous chapters to a measurement outside the brain. A memory coordinate can diffuse inside a neural network, but the movement produced by that coordinate also depends on the muscles and the mechanics of the eye. We need to follow the signal through those stages before comparing a neural diffusion law with an eye trajectory. A recording from one motor neuron becomes useful for this comparison only after its spikes and the eye's movement can be expressed on the same scale. The larger movements provide that calibration. Applying it during fixation then lets us ask whether independent motor noise could explain the observed relationship, and estimate the shared contribution under explicit gain and independence assumptions. ## From stored eye position to muscle action {#sec:EYE-PATHWAY} The eye needs an ongoing command to maintain a position. A brief command to move is therefore insufficient: after the movement, a circuit must maintain activity representing the new position. [The [**oculomotor integrator**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} is the neural circuit that performs this storage. “Integrator” refers to turning a movement command into a lasting position signal.]{.definition-explanation} In the proposed mechanism, the continuous attractor described in the [foundations](ch-persistence.html#sec-foundations-attractor) and [network model](ch-memory-dynamics.html#sec-memory-spikes) stores horizontal eye position. Noise moves the stored value along that attractor.[^p2-pathway] [The signal reaches [**ocular motoneurons (OMNs)**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}, neurons whose spikes activate the eye muscles.]{.definition-explanation} [The recordings came from the [**abducens nucleus**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}, a group of brainstem neurons that includes OMNs activating the lateral rectus muscle, which turns the eye outward.]{.definition-explanation} Other neurons in that nucleus carry signals to other neurons rather than directly to muscle. The study separated these cell types by how their firing changed with eye position and movement. [Finally, the muscles and the mechanical properties of the eye, together called the [**ocular plant**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}, turn neural activity into movement.]{.definition-explanation}[^p2-recordings]
Original paper figure: Ben-Shushan et al. (2022), Extended Data Figure 6
{{block:fig:PAPER-EYE-ED6}}
There are three possible contributions to an observed drift: - A changing shared command sent to many OMNs. - Private spike variability in individual OMNs. - Variability after those neurons, including muscle and measurement noise. [Private spike fluctuations can partly cancel when many neurons act together. A common command survives this averaging.]{.key-statement} This is why the noisy activity of one neuron can reveal a source that dominates the much smoother eye movement. ## The recordings pair one motor neuron with movement at a time {#sec:EYE-RECORDINGS} The authors reanalyzed earlier experiments in two male rhesus macaques. With their heads held still, the monkeys first looked at a stationary spot of light on a monitor and then followed the moving spot. A wire search coil on one eye measured the eye's angle while an electrode recorded one neuron's spikes. There were 57 identified OMNs. [Each recording paired one OMN with eye movement. There were no simultaneous recordings of multiple OMNs. Thus the analysis cannot directly measure the covariance between two recorded motor neurons.]{.key-statement}[^p2-recordings][^p2-single] The initial stationary target was followed by 500–700 ms of required fixation before the target stepped and began moving. Neural voltage was sampled at 25 kHz and eye position at 1 kHz. The authors detected microsaccades using eye speed and acceleration, removed 30 ms on each side of them, and manually checked the remaining segments. For the main displacement analysis, segments shorter than 350 ms were excluded and longer ones were split into nonoverlapping 350 ms pieces. There were 302 such pieces per cell on average, with different counts across cells. These repeated observations improve estimates within two animals. They do not create 57 independent animal samples.[^p2-segments]
Original paper figure: Ben-Shushan et al. (2022), Extended Data Figure 7
{{block:fig:PAPER-EYE-ED7}}
The large movements have a useful role even though the scientific question concerns tiny drifts. They produce enough rate change to estimate how each cell's activity depends on eye movement. The fitted relationship is then applied during fixation. This transfer is an assumption to examine, because an incorrect gain during drift would change the inferred common variance. Gain is the scale that converts a change in one signal into a change in the other.
{{block:fig:EYE-PHYSICAL-AND-RECORDED}}
## A fitted model links movement to firing rate {#sec:EYE-FORWARD-FIT} Position alone does not predict a motor neuron's activity during a movement. At the same position, firing can differ when the eye is moving or accelerating. The paper therefore fits $$ \widehat f(t)=k[E(t+\Delta t)-E_T] +r\dot E(t+\Delta t)+m\ddot E(t+\Delta t). $$ Here $E$ is horizontal eye position in degrees and $\widehat f$ is predicted firing rate in spikes/s. The position threshold $E_T$ sets where the position term reaches zero. The coefficients have units $$ [k]=\frac{\text{spikes}}{\text{s}\,\text{deg}},\qquad [r]=\frac{\text{spikes}}{\text{deg}},\qquad [m]=\frac{\text{spikes}\,\text{s}}{\text{deg}}. $$ Multiplying by position, velocity, and acceleration gives spikes/s in all three terms. The position term describes ongoing firing associated with holding the eye at an angle. The velocity term allows a different rate while the eye passes through that same angle. The acceleration term allows another change while its velocity changes. Thus $k$, $r$, and $m$ describe different demands on the motor signal. They are fitted coefficients of the combined neural and mechanical relationship. In particular, $m$ is not a direct measurement of the eye's mass. The delay $\Delta t$ is in seconds: firing at time $t$ predicts movement at the later time $t+\Delta t$ for a positive neural lead. This is the paper's Eq. 2, including its threshold and time shift.[^p2-forward] The observed rate $f(t)$ was estimated as the inverse of the interval between successive spikes, constant between those spikes. For each cell, the authors minimized the sum of squared rate errors, $$ L=\sum_{a=1}^{n_{\rm trials}}\sum_{t_j\in[0,T_a]} \left[f_a(t_j)-\widehat f_a(t_j;k,r,m,\Delta t,E_T)\right]^2. $$ $a$ labels trials and $T_a$ is trial duration. This is Eq. 3 with the trial count renamed so that it cannot be confused with a neuron count. Fits used full trials, including fixation and pursuit. To predict a trial's rate, that trial was left out of the parameter fit. Acceleration was estimated from velocity after local polynomial smoothing over 21 ms. Trials in which the rate fell below 20 Hz were discarded: the linear formula is intended for active cells above firing threshold, whereas firing cannot become negative.[^p2-forward] During fixation, the authors subtracted each segment's mean firing rate, joined the segments, and compared observed and predicted rate fluctuations. Figure 1c illustrates a weak relationship for one cell. Fig. 1d shows a positive population effect. The one sided test asks whether the mean correlation is positive, compared with a zero-mean reference. [Its [**p value**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} is the probability, under that reference, of a test statistic at least as large as observed.]{.definition-explanation} Across 57 cells it gave $p=3\times10^{-9}$. A weak single cell relationship is expected here because the tiny movement produces small rate changes against much larger spike variability. This is the first evidence of a relationship, before any estimate of the fraction of common motion.[^p2-rate-result]
Original paper figure: Ben-Shushan et al. (2022), Figure 1
{{block:fig:PAPER-EYE-1}}
## A calibrated filter predicts eye position from one cell's spikes {#sec:EYE-INVERSE-FILTER} To ask how much eye movement is shared with a neuron, it helps to express both signals in degrees. [The paper reverses the fitted relationship: a cell's spike train becomes the input, and its prediction of eye position becomes the output. This operation is an inverse of the movement-to-rate fit, rather than a new fit to small drift residuals.]{.key-statement} Let $x(t)=E(t)-E_T$. Ignoring the time shift for a moment, the deterministic relation is $$ m\ddot x+r\dot x+kx=f. $$ [A [**causal filter**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} computes its present output from present and past input. For the equation above, its [**impulse response**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} $h_0(u)$ is the position response to one instantaneous spike at time zero.]{.definition-explanation} To factor the equation, consider a time component $e^{pt}$: differentiation multiplies it by $p$. The algebraic ratio of output to input for that component is $$ H_0(p)=\frac{1}{mp^2+rp+k} =\frac{1}{m(p+1/\tau_+)(p+1/\tau_-)}. $$ Factoring the quadratic gives the slow and fast decay times $$ \tau_+=\frac{2}{r/m-\sqrt{(r/m)^2-4k/m}},\qquad \tau_-=\frac{2}{r/m+\sqrt{(r/m)^2-4k/m}}. $$ These are the paired signs in the paper's Eq. 7, with $\tau_+>\tau_-$ when $k,r,m>0$ and $r^2>4km$. Under these conditions both components decay without oscillation. At rest, the inverse equation gives $x=f/k$: with the threshold fixed, doubling $k$ halves the position offset predicted from the same steady firing rate. During a change, $r$ and $m$ also affect the response through the two timescales. This is a consequence of the fitted relationship, not evidence that changing one recorded neuron's rate alone sets eye position. The same factorization gives two useful identities: $$ \tau_+\tau_-=\frac{m}{k},\qquad \tau_++\tau_-=\frac{r}{k}. $$ The corresponding impulse response is $$ h_0(u)=\frac{\Theta(u)}{m}\, \frac{\tau_+\tau_-}{\tau_+-\tau_-} \left(e^{-u/\tau_+}-e^{-u/\tau_-}\right). $$ $\Theta(u)$ is zero for $u<0$ and one for $u>0$, which makes the response zero before the input. Restoring the fitted neural lead delays this response: $h(u)=h_0(u-\Delta t)$. Write the spike train as $\xi(t)=\sum_j\delta(t-t_j)$, where $\delta$ is an ideal instantaneous impulse of unit area, so integration over one spike counts one event. The prediction is $$ \widehat E(t)=E_T+\int_{-\infty}^{t}h(t-v)\xi(v)\,dv =E_T+\sum_j h(t-t_j). $$ These expressions reproduce Eqs. 4–6, including the factor $\tau_+\tau_-/m$ and the delay. [The [**convolution**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} integral adds the responses to all past spikes.]{.definition-explanation} With spike count treated as a count, $\xi$ has units spikes/s and $h$ has units degrees/spike. Each spike contributes a decaying position response. Adding those responses produces degrees.[^p2-inversion] ::: {.publisher-clarification-note .publisher-fold-always title="Derivation: the weights of the two decaying responses"} We can obtain the response to a spike directly from the differential equation. After the spike, the input is zero, and each of the two exponentials solves the remaining homogeneous equation. Write their combination as $$ h_0(u)=A e^{-u/\tau_+}+B e^{-u/\tau_-},\qquad u>0. $$ To find $A$ and $B$, treat the spike as a short pulse of unit area and shrink its duration to zero. The position change during that pulse tends to zero, so $h_0(0^+)=0$. Integrating $m h_0''+r h_0'+k h_0$ across the pulse gives $m h_0'(0^+)=1$: the velocity changes by $1/m$, while position and velocity before the causal response are zero. Therefore $$ A+B=0,\qquad -\frac{A}{\tau_+}-\frac{B}{\tau_-}=\frac1m. $$ Substituting $B=-A$ gives $A(1/\tau_- -1/\tau_+)=1/m$, hence $A=\tau_+\tau_-/[m(\tau_+-\tau_-)]$. Making the response zero before the spike gives the impulse response $h_0(u)$. ::: For a constructed example, take $k=4$ spikes/(s deg), $\tau_+=0.120$ s, and $\tau_-=0.005$ s. The identities above require $r=0.500$ spikes/deg and $m=0.00240$ spikes s/deg. Then $$ h_0(u)=2.174\left(e^{-u/0.120}-e^{-u/0.005}\right) \ \text{deg/spike},\quad u>0, $$ and its area is $2.174(0.120-0.005)=0.250$ deg s/spike, equal to $1/k$. A steady rate of 80 spikes/s predicts an offset of 20 degrees above $E_T$. This checks the gain and the time constants. ::: {.publisher-clarification-note .publisher-fold-always title="Check: static gain and equal decay times"} The kernel's area checks its normalization: $$ \int_0^\infty h_0(u)\,du =\frac{\tau_+\tau_-}{m(\tau_+-\tau_-)}(\tau_+-\tau_-) =\frac1k. $$ Thus a constant input rate $f_0$ predicts $E_T+f_0/k$, exactly the static forward relation. A kernel with unit area would give the wrong conversion unless $k$ had already been absorbed into the input. When the two decay times coincide, $r^2=4km$, the limit is $h_0(u)=\Theta(u)u e^{-u/\tau}/m$. The distinct exponential formula is used for the fitted responses in the paper. ::: Figure 2a–b shows typical fitted times of about 5 ms and 120 ms. Figure 2c shows that a single cell's reconstructed drift is much noisier than the measured movement. Across 350 ms displacement pairs, the mean Pearson correlation was $\langle R\rangle=0.17\pm0.02$, [where the error is the [**standard error of the mean (SEM)**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}. SEM estimates uncertainty in the across-cell mean, rather than the spread of individual cells or uncertainty across animals.]{.definition-explanation} The one sided test gave $p=3.8\times10^{-12}$. Shuffling which measured segment was paired with which spike prediction centered the comparison near zero. Here and below $\langle\cdot\rangle$ over cells means a population average.[^p2-correlation]
Original paper figure: Ben-Shushan et al. (2022), Figure 2
{{block:fig:PAPER-EYE-2}}
## The measured correlation challenges independent motor noise alone {#sec:EYE-SHARED-VARIANCE} A correlation of 0.17 does not immediately tell us how much motion comes from the common command. First we can ask a more limited question: could all the motion come from independent motor neuron fluctuations? For a centered displacement $Y$ and one centered prediction $X$, the best linear prediction $bX$ minimizes $\operatorname{Var}(Y-bX)$. Differentiating with respect to $b$ gives $b=\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)/\operatorname{Var}(X)$. Its explained fraction of variance is $$ \frac{b^2\operatorname{Var}(X)}{\operatorname{Var}(Y)} =\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)^2}{\operatorname{Var}(X)\operatorname{Var}(Y)} =R^2. $$ [This is the [**coefficient of determination**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} for a linear prediction with a fitted gain.]{.definition-explanation} It does not assert that the raw, unscaled position predictor itself has a small squared error. Suppose there are $N_m$ independent single neuron predictors $X_i$. Standardize each to variance one and also standardize $Y$. Independence makes the $X_i$ uncorrelated, so the residual after using them all has variance $$ \operatorname{Var}\left(Y-\sum_i R_iX_i\right) =1-2\sum_iR_i^2+\sum_iR_i^2 =1-\sum_iR_i^2\ge0. $$ Consequently $\sum_iR_i^2\le1$, and an average neuron explains at most $1/N_m$. This proves the bound used in Supplementary Eq. S1. It does not require equal muscle effects from all neurons. Applying it to the sampled cells does require their average explanatory power to represent the relevant motor population.[^p2-independent-bound] The authors avoid directly averaging noisy squared correlations. Instead, $$ \langle R^2\rangle-\langle R\rangle^2=\operatorname{Var}(R)\ge0, \qquad \langle R^2\rangle\ge(0.17)^2=0.0289. $$ [Thus the estimated mean correlation implies an average explained fraction of at least about 2.9%. For 1,000 independently contributing motor neurons, the bound would be 0.1%. For several thousand it is smaller. The mismatch argues against independent OMN noise as the sole source.]{.key-statement} Shared fluctuations can allow many cells to explain the same part of the movement, so their explained fractions can overlap.[^p2-independent-bound] This step finds shared variation. Locating its source upstream also uses a biological premise: the private variability generated within OMNs is taken to be independent across cells. The paper supports that premise using anatomical and stimulation studies indicating little local recurrent coupling in the relevant motor nuclei. It was not tested by simultaneous recordings in this data set. Common inputs can correlate the total activity of OMNs even when their privately generated spike noise is independent.[^p2-independence] ## Calibrated covariance estimates the common share of movement variance {#sec:EYE-CHI} The variance bound establishes that a shared signal exists, but leaves its size open. The next calculation uses the inverse filter’s calibrated gain in degrees. For one 350 ms interval, write the measured displacement and the single cell prediction as $$ Y=\delta E=C+\eta,\qquad X=\delta\widehat E=C+\epsilon, $$ where $C=\delta E_C$ is the common upstream contribution, $\eta$ combines motor neuron, muscle, and measurement contributions to measured displacement, and $\epsilon$ is the prediction error from the individual cell. All are displacement variables in degrees. The calculation assumes: - The common contribution enters both signals with unit gain, meaning the same one-for-one displacement scale. - $C,\eta,\epsilon$ are pairwise uncorrelated to the required accuracy. Expanding the covariance shows why those assumptions matter: $$ \operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=\operatorname{Var}(C) +\operatorname{Cov}(C,\eta)+\operatorname{Cov}(\epsilon,C) +\operatorname{Cov}(\epsilon,\eta) \simeq\operatorname{Var}(C). $$ The common fraction is therefore estimated by $$ \chi=\frac{\operatorname{Var}(C)}{\operatorname{Var}(Y)} \simeq\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)}{\operatorname{Var}(Y)}. $$ These are Eqs. 11–15 in displacement form. The gain assumption requires that the relation calibrated during larger movements still applies during drift. There is also a small covariance between $\epsilon$ and $\eta$, because the recorded neuron's private spikes contribute both to its predictor and to actual eye motion. The paper neglects this contribution as order $1/N_m$ under its many neuron model.[^p2-chi-method] Correlation divides the same covariance by a different denominator: $$ R=\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)}{\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(X)\operatorname{Var}(Y)}}, \qquad \chi\simeq R\sqrt{\frac{\operatorname{Var}(X)}{\operatorname{Var}(Y)}}. $$ [Large private noise in a cell inflates $\operatorname{Var}(X)$ and makes $R$ small. It need not make the common contribution to the real movement small, because many independent private contributions average down there.]{.key-statement}
**Example: correlation 0.17 with a common fraction 0.82.** These numbers are constructed to expose the distinction, not extracted from individual cells. Take independent centered variables with $$ \operatorname{Var}(C)=0.00820\ \text{deg}^2,\quad \operatorname{Var}(\eta)=0.00180\ \text{deg}^2,\quad \operatorname{Var}(\epsilon)=0.22446\ \text{deg}^2. $$ Then $\operatorname{Var}(Y)=0.01000$, $\operatorname{Var}(X)=0.23266$, and $\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=0.00820$, all in deg$^2$. It follows that $$ R=\frac{0.00820}{\sqrt{0.01000\times0.23266}}\simeq0.170, \qquad \chi=\frac{0.00820}{0.01000}=0.820. $$ One cell explains $R^2\simeq2.89\%$ of displacement variance after linear rescaling, while the common signal supplies 82% of actual displacement variance. The larger, poorly predicted part of the single cell signal is private prediction noise.
{{block:fig:EYE-SHARED-PRIVATE-VARIANCE}}
The bars use the same physical scale, so the equal common pieces have equal lengths. See [Shared and private variability, Eqs. 11–15, p. 10](../papers/ben-shushan-2022-fixational-drift.pdf#page=10).
In the experiment, each cell gives a noisy estimate $\chi_i$, and those estimates can lie outside $[0,1]$. The underlying variance fraction remains in that interval under the model, but the sample covariance need not. The paper estimates each standard error $\Delta\chi_i$ mainly from covariance uncertainty, treating the measured displacement variance in the denominator as comparatively well determined. It then uses inverse variance weighting: $$ w_i=\frac{1}{(\Delta\chi_i)^2},\qquad \widehat\chi=\frac{\sum_iw_i\chi_i}{\sum_iw_i},\qquad \sigma_{\widehat\chi}=\left(\sum_iw_i\right)^{-1/2}. $$ To see the weighting, let normalized weights $a_i$ sum to one. Independent errors give variance $\sum_i a_i^2(\Delta\chi_i)^2$ for $\sum_i a_i\chi_i$. Minimizing this subject to $\sum_i a_i=1$ gives $a_i\propto1/(\Delta\chi_i)^2$ and the error above. The paper additionally assumes approximately normal errors around a common value. The last expression is a propagated estimation error under those assumptions. It does not measure variation across animals or uncertainty in the gain and independence assumptions. paragraphs.text: <!-- vale ai-tells.FillerIntensifier = NO --> The shared movement estimate concerns a single interval length. [It leaves open whether the command merely fluctuates around a stable value or keeps accumulating changes. Comparing displacements over different time separations can distinguish these possibilities, but the smallest measured displacements may include a large contribution from recording error.]{.key-statement} <!-- vale ai-tells.FillerIntensifier = YES -->

The mean squared displacement measures the average squared position change over a chosen interval. Separating the recording error from that quantity is necessary before interpreting its growth. To test whether the command accumulates changes, we compare two possible inputs after a decaying muscle response: fluctuations that do not accumulate and a position that wanders by diffusion. Their different long interval behavior explains how a smooth eye movement can still reflect a wandering stored value.

review_metadata.title: Drift growth distinguishes diffusion from filtered white noise
review_metadata.purpose: Eye movements recorded during steady gaze in monkeys look different over short and long time intervals. This chapter uses their timing to distinguish fluctuations around a fixed command from accumulated changes in the command, while accounting for eye-position measurement error.

blocks.caption: Filtering stationary white input produces an MSD plateau; filtering Brownian stored position preserves long-lag growth. Each panel uses its own normalization, $M_{\mathrm{white}}/(A/\tau)$ and $M_{\mathrm{Brownian}}/(2D\tau)$, so the figure compares shapes without matching physical noise amplitudes. Original guide calculation for the one-pole teaching model, connected to Ben-Shushan et al. (2022), Fig. 3 and main Eqs. 20–22; these are not measured data or the fitted full-model curves.
blocks.alt: Two alternative inputs pass through identical one-pole filters. On matched logarithmic lag axes x equals lag divided by tau, normalized white-input MSD is 1 minus exp(-x), rising with short-lag slope one and approaching a plateau of one. Independently normalized filtered Brownian MSD is x minus one plus exp(-x), starting with slope two and continuing to grow with long-lag slope one. The two vertical scales differ.

blocks.caption: For positive lags, independent measurement error adds $2\sigma_m^2$ to the movement MSD, here $M(\ell)=2D\ell$. The isolated point at zero lag stays zero because each sample is subtracted from itself. At 20 ms, subtracting 0.0010 from 0.0014 deg² leaves 0.0004 deg²; the shown ±0.0001 deg² subtraction uncertainty is 25% of that remainder. Original analytic example, not experimental data, using Ben-Shushan et al. (2022), main p. 10, Eqs. 18–19.
blocks.alt: Movement MSD rises linearly from zero. For all strictly positive lags, observed MSD is higher by 0.0010 degrees squared. The observed curve has an open endpoint at lag zero, above the actual zero-lag point at zero. # Drift growth distinguishes diffusion from filtered white noise {#ch:EYE-TIMING} The shared movement estimate concerns a single interval length. [It leaves open whether the command merely fluctuates around a stable value or keeps accumulating changes. Comparing displacements over different time separations can distinguish these possibilities, but the smallest measured displacements may include a large contribution from recording error.]{.key-statement} The mean squared displacement measures the average squared position change over a chosen interval. Separating the recording error from that quantity is necessary before interpreting its growth. To test whether the command accumulates changes, we compare two possible inputs after a decaying muscle response: fluctuations that do not accumulate and a position that wanders by diffusion. Their different long interval behavior explains how a smooth eye movement can still reflect a wandering stored value. ## Independent measurement error adds a constant offset to the MSD {#sec:EYE-MEASUREMENT-NOISE} The common variance calculation uses one interval length. To learn what kind of process drives motion, the authors next compare displacements at many time separations. Using the [earlier definition of mean squared displacement](ch-foundations.html#sec-foundations-covariance), $$ M(\ell)=\mathbb E\{[E(t+\ell)-E(t)]^2\} $$ is the mean squared displacement, or MSD, at lag $\ell$. The data estimate it within each microsaccade free segment, then average the available segment estimates at each lag. Larger lags have fewer eligible segments. The 1 ms sampling sets the available lag spacing.[^p2-msd] At short lags, the displacement can be smaller than the search coil's measurement error. Suppose its reading is $E_{\rm obs}(t)=E(t)+\nu(t)$. The measurement error is assumed to have: - Zero mean and variance $\sigma_m^2$. - Independence from true movement. - No correlation between distinct sampled times. For a positive lag, $$ \begin{aligned} M_{\rm obs}(\ell) &=\mathbb E[(\delta E+\delta\nu)^2]\\ &=M(\ell)+\mathbb E[\nu(t+\ell)^2]+\mathbb E[\nu(t)^2] -2\mathbb E[\nu(t+\ell)\nu(t)]\\ &=M(\ell)+2\sigma_m^2. \end{aligned} $$ The mixed movement-error term vanishes by independence. This is Eqs. 18–19. The correction is the variance of a difference of two errors, $2\sigma_m^2$, rather than the variance of a single position error. At exactly zero lag the same error is subtracted from itself, so the MSD is zero. A positive lag plateau near zero lag can still occur when successive measurement errors are independent.[^p2-msd-noise] The authors estimated the plateau contribution at order $10^{-3}$ deg$^2$, checked its scale with a coil fixed in space, and subtracted that contribution from the observed MSD. [This is a correction of an average statistic, not knowledge of each trial's unknown noise.]{.key-statement} Smoothing the eye trajectories instead would also change the movement statistics the analysis seeks to measure. If the plateau estimate has uncertainty $10^{-4}$ deg$^2$, a corrected MSD of that size is unreliable even when the plateau itself is much larger. The peer review response uses this example to explain the shortest lag limitation.[^p2-noise-limit]
Original paper figure: Ben-Shushan et al. (2022), Extended Data Figure 2
{{block:fig:PAPER-EYE-ED2}}
For instance, a constructed measured MSD of $0.0014$ deg$^2$ with an estimated noise contribution $0.0010$ deg$^2$ leaves $0.0004$ deg$^2$. A $0.0001$ deg$^2$ uncertainty in the subtraction is already 25% of that result. This is why a corrected short lag point needs an uncertainty assessment as well as a positive value. If measurement errors were temporally correlated, the correction would instead be $2[\sigma_m^2-C_\nu(\ell)]$, where $C_\nu$ is their covariance at lag $\ell$. A constant subtraction would then need revision. For a constructed Brownian movement with $D=0.010$ deg$^2$/s, adding independent position measurement errors with $2\sigma_m^2=0.0010$ deg$^2$ shifts every positive-lag MSD upward by the same amount.
{{block:fig:EYE-MSD-MEASUREMENT-OFFSET}}
The Brownian movement is chosen only to make the constant offset visible. See [Measurement noise correction, Eqs. 18–19, p. 10](../papers/ben-shushan-2022-fixational-drift.pdf#page=10). ## The MSD plateaus for filtered white noise but grows for filtered diffusion {#sec:EYE-FILTERED-MSD} The corrected MSD keeps increasing over the observed range, toward a second, while its logarithmic slope decreases and remains between one and two. Define that local slope by $$ \alpha(\ell)=\frac{d\log M(\ell)}{d\log\ell} =\frac{\ell M'(\ell)}{M(\ell)}. $$ Ordinary diffusion has $M=2D\ell$ and $\alpha=1$. A roughly constant velocity over a short interval gives displacement $v\ell$ and $M=\mathbb E[v^2]\ell^2$, so $\alpha=2$. [Growth faster than linear is called [**superdiffusion**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}. Here it describes a finite range of lags. It does not assert a single power law for arbitrarily long times.]{.definition-explanation}[^p2-msd-result] Could temporally uncorrelated motor noise acquire the observed MSD just by passing through muscles? [A [**low pass filter**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} suppresses rapid input changes relative to slow ones.]{.definition-explanation} [[**White noise**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} here is an ideal zero mean input whose fluctuations at different times are uncorrelated. In continuous time its strength is defined by an intensity multiplying a delta function, rather than a finite variance at an individual time.]{.definition-explanation} [A stable, decaying response to this noise produces a [**stationary process**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} in the sense needed here: its mean is constant and its covariance depends only on time separation.]{.definition-explanation} Its position variance consequently does not grow with absolute time. Let $E=h*\xi$, where $$ \mathbb E[\xi(t)\xi(t')]=A\delta(t-t'). $$ The noise intensity $A$ has units input$^2$ times seconds. Expanding the convolution and using the delta function yields, for $\ell\ge0$, $$ C_E(\ell)=\mathbb E[E(t)E(t+\ell)] =A\int_0^\infty h(u)h(u+\ell)\,du. $$ For a stationary centered position, expanding the squared difference then gives $$ M(\ell)=2[C_E(0)-C_E(\ell)]. $$ If the kernel decays sufficiently rapidly, its overlap with a shifted copy tends to zero. The MSD consequently approaches $2C_E(0)$, a finite plateau. This reconstructs the reasoning of Eqs. 20–22.[^p2-white-noise] For the one exponential filter $h(u)=\Theta(u)e^{-u/\tau}/\tau$, $$ C_E(\ell)=\frac{A}{2\tau}e^{-\ell/\tau},\qquad M_{\rm white}(\ell)=\frac A\tau(1-e^{-\ell/\tau}). $$ This simple filter has a short lag MSD proportional to $\ell$ and a long lag plateau. A double exponential filter is smoother at short lags, but still gives a plateau because its kernel also decays. Increasing $A$ raises the curve without removing its flattening. The paper's simulated private OMN noise, passed through muscle dynamics, is both too small and too flat at long lags. In Fig. 3b, using 2,000 heterogeneous OMNs, its contribution is about 1% of the observed variance near 900 ms.[^p2-msd-result]
Original paper figure: Ben-Shushan et al. (2022), Figure 3
{{block:fig:PAPER-EYE-3}}
Filtered white noise cannot explain continued long-lag growth. Suppose instead the input is a stored position $B(t)$ undergoing Brownian motion with $\mathbb E[(B(t+\ell)-B(t))^2]=2D\ell$. Its position variance accumulates. A low pass filter with nonzero static gain smooths the path while retaining that accumulating long time displacement variance. The following one exponential example is a teaching reconstruction, not the paper's full muscle model. It derives how smooth movement can have a slope between one and two even though the stored position undergoes ordinary diffusion. Let $$ \tau\dot E+E=B,\qquad dB=\sqrt{2D}\,dW. $$ Here $B$ is the changing position command and $E$ is the eye angle that follows it, both in degrees. The mismatch $B-E$ drives velocity: a command to the right of the current position makes the eye move right. For the same mismatch, a larger response time $\tau$ gives a smaller velocity, so the eye takes longer to catch up and smooths rapid command changes more strongly. This response time belongs to the simplified eye filter. It is not automatically the synaptic decay time used in the memory model. $W$ is a Brownian process with unit increment variance per unit time, so $D$ has units deg$^2$/s. Define velocity $v=\dot E=(B-E)/\tau$. Taking its increment gives $$ \tau\,dv=-v\,dt+\sqrt{2D}\,dW. $$ Velocity loses its past value over time $\tau$ and receives new random input. To add the surviving effect of those inputs, divide the past into short intervals of width $h$. The Brownian change $\Delta W_j=W(u_j+h)-W(u_j)$ has mean zero and variance $h$. Changes in disjoint intervals are independent. Its contribution to the velocity at time $t$ is approximately $(\sqrt{2D}/\tau)e^{-(t-u_j)/\tau}\Delta W_j$: the initial change has decayed between $u_j$ and $t$. The integral against $dW(u)$ denotes the limit of these weighted sums as $h$ tends to zero. It does not require an ordinary derivative of the Brownian path. After the initial velocity has decayed, extending the input history into the distant past gives $$ v(t)=\frac{\sqrt{2D}}{\tau}\int_{-\infty}^{t}e^{-(t-u)/\tau}\,dW(u). $$ For a lag $s\geq0$, multiply the sums for $v(t)$ and $v(t+s)$ and average. Products of distinct increments have zero mean. The same increment contributes its variance $h$, so the sum becomes an ordinary overlap integral over their shared past: $$ \begin{aligned} C_v(s) &=\frac{2D}{\tau^2}\int_{-\infty}^{t} e^{-(t-u)/\tau}e^{-(t+s-u)/\tau}\,du\\ &=\frac{2D}{\tau^2}e^{-s/\tau}\int_0^\infty e^{-2r/\tau}\,dr =\frac D\tau e^{-s/\tau}. \end{aligned} $$ Here $r=t-u$ is the age of an input increment. Covariance is even in the lag, so $C_v(s)=(D/\tau)e^{-|s|/\tau}$ for either sign of $s$. Integrating velocity over an interval gives position change. The double integral over its covariance reduces to $$ \begin{aligned} M_{\rm Brownian}(\ell) &=\int_0^\ell\int_0^\ell C_v(u-v)\,du\,dv\\ &=2\int_0^\ell(\ell-s)C_v(s)\,ds\\ &=2D[\ell-\tau(1-e^{-\ell/\tau})]. \end{aligned} $$ At short lags, $1-e^{-\ell/\tau}=\ell/\tau-\ell^2/(2\tau^2)+\cdots$, so $$ M_{\rm Brownian}(\ell)\simeq(D/\tau)\ell^2. $$ The eye keeps approximately the same velocity over that interval. At long lags, $$ M_{\rm Brownian}(\ell)\simeq2D(\ell-\tau), $$ which grows linearly rather than approaching a plateau. Holding the internal diffusion coefficient $D$ fixed, increasing $\tau$ reduces short-lag displacement and moves the transition to linear growth to longer lags. It does not stop accumulating error: the long-lag MSD growth rate still approaches $2D$. Increasing $D$ instead raises the entire MSD curve in proportion, at fixed $\tau$. The local logarithmic slope of this MSD is $$ \alpha(\ell)=\frac{\ell(1-e^{-\ell/\tau})} {\ell-\tau(1-e^{-\ell/\tau})}, $$ approaching two at short lags and one at long lags. At $\ell=\tau$ it is $e-1\simeq1.718$. At $\ell=5\tau$ it is about $1.239$. [Thus an intermediate slope can arise from filtering ordinary diffusion, without faster than Brownian accumulation inside the memory circuit.]{.key-statement} The curves compare the two inputs after the same filter with one exponential response, also called a one pole filter.
{{block:fig:EYE-FILTERED-NOISE-MSD}}
The white-input short-lag slope of one belongs to this one-pole example. The actual muscle response contains fast and slow exponential components, and the full model also contains motor neuron filtering and feedback. Those ingredients change the detailed curve. The one exponential derivation teaches the distinction relevant to Fig. 3: [a decaying low pass filter of stationary white noise saturates, whereas the same filter, with nonzero static gain, retains accumulating displacement from a wandering position. A slow correlated peripheral source is a different hypothesis from the temporally uncorrelated noise rejected by this comparison.]{.key-statement} [^p2-msd]: Ben-Shushan, N., Shaham, N., Joshua, M., & Burak, Y. (2022). *Fixational drift is driven by diffusive dynamics in central neural circuitry*. Nature Communications, 13, 1697. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-022-29201-y). Main p. 10, “Calculation of empirical MSD.” [^p2-msd-noise]: Ben-Shushan, N., Shaham, N., Joshua, M., & Burak, Y. (2022). *Fixational drift is driven by diffusive dynamics in central neural circuitry*. Nature Communications, 13, 1697. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-022-29201-y). Main p. 10, “Removal of measurement noise,” Eqs. 18–19; Supplementary Information, p. 8, Extended Data Fig. 2. The plotted plateau is the displacement noise contribution, twice the single position noise variance. [^p2-noise-limit]: Ben-Shushan, N., Shaham, N., Joshua, M., & Burak, Y. (2022). *Fixational drift is driven by diffusive dynamics in central neural circuitry*. Nature Communications, 13, 1697, peer review file, pp. 20–21, measurement noise subtraction, uncertainty example, and short lag restriction. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-022-29201-y). [^p2-msd-result]: Ben-Shushan, N., Shaham, N., Joshua, M., & Burak, Y. (2022). *Fixational drift is driven by diffusive dynamics in central neural circuitry*. Nature Communications, 13, 1697. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-022-29201-y). Main pp. 5–6, “Central source” timing argument and Fig. 3. [^p2-white-noise]: Ben-Shushan, N., Shaham, N., Joshua, M., & Burak, Y. (2022). *Fixational drift is driven by diffusive dynamics in central neural circuitry*. Nature Communications, 13, 1697. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-022-29201-y). Main p. 10, “MSD curve of low-pass filtered white noise,” Eqs. 20–22. The normalized one exponential example and filtered Brownian derivation are teaching reconstructions.

review_metadata.title: Drift growth distinguishes diffusion from filtered white noise
review_metadata.purpose: Eye movements recorded during steady gaze in monkeys look different over short and long time intervals. This chapter uses their timing to distinguish fluctuations around a fixed command from accumulated changes in the command, while accounting for eye-position measurement error.

Using the [earlier definition of mean squared displacement](ch-foundations.html#sec-foundations-covariance), $$ M(\ell)=\mathbb E\{[E(t+\ell)-E(t)]^2\} $$ is the mean squared displacement, or MSD, at lag $\ell$. The data estimate it within each microsaccade free segment, then average the available segment estimates at each lag. Larger lags have fewer eligible segments. The 1 ms sampling sets the available lag spacing.[^p2-msd] At short lags, the displacement can be smaller than the search coil's measurement error. Suppose its reading is $E_{\rm obs}(t)=E(t)+\nu(t)$. The measurement error is assumed to have: - Zero mean and variance $\sigma_m^2$. - Independence from true movement. - No correlation between distinct sampled times. For a positive lag, $$ \begin{aligned} M_{\rm obs}(\ell) &=\mathbb E[(\delta E+\delta\nu)^2]\\ &=M(\ell)+\mathbb E[\nu(t+\ell)^2]+\mathbb E[\nu(t)^2] -2\mathbb E[\nu(t+\ell)\nu(t)]\\ &=M(\ell)+2\sigma_m^2. \end{aligned} $$ The mixed movement-error term vanishes by independence. This is Eqs. 18–19. The correction is the variance of a difference of two errors, $2\sigma_m^2$, rather than the variance of a single position error. At exactly zero lag the same error is subtracted from itself, so the MSD is zero. A positive lag plateau near zero lag can still occur when successive measurement errors are independent.[^p2-msd-noise] The authors estimated the plateau contribution at order $10^{-3}$ deg$^2$, checked its scale with a coil fixed in space, and subtracted that contribution from the observed MSD. [This is a correction of an average statistic, not knowledge of each trial's unknown noise.]{.key-statement} Smoothing the eye trajectories instead would also change the movement statistics the analysis seeks to measure. If the plateau estimate has uncertainty $10^{-4}$ deg$^2$, a corrected MSD of that size is unreliable even when the plateau itself is much larger. The peer review response uses this example to explain the shortest lag limitation.[^p2-noise-limit]
Original paper figure: Ben-Shushan et al. (2022), Extended Data Figure 2
{{block:fig:PAPER-EYE-ED2}}
For instance, a constructed measured MSD of $0.0014$ deg$^2$ with an estimated noise contribution $0.0010$ deg$^2$ leaves $0.0004$ deg$^2$. A $0.0001$ deg$^2$ uncertainty in the subtraction is already 25% of that result. This is why a corrected short lag point needs an uncertainty assessment as well as a positive value. If measurement errors were temporally correlated, the correction would instead be $2[\sigma_m^2-C_\nu(\ell)]$, where $C_\nu$ is their covariance at lag $\ell$. A constant subtraction would then need revision. For a constructed Brownian movement with $D=0.010$ deg$^2$/s, adding independent position measurement errors with $2\sigma_m^2=0.0010$ deg$^2$ shifts every positive-lag MSD upward by the same amount.
{{block:fig:EYE-MSD-MEASUREMENT-OFFSET}}
The Brownian movement is chosen only to make the constant offset visible. See [Measurement noise correction, Eqs. 18–19, p. 10](../papers/ben-shushan-2022-fixational-drift.pdf#page=10). ## The MSD plateaus for filtered white noise but grows for filtered diffusion {#sec:EYE-FILTERED-MSD} The corrected MSD keeps increasing over the observed range, toward a second, while its logarithmic slope decreases and remains between one and two. Define that local slope by $$ \alpha(\ell)=\frac{d\log M(\ell)}{d\log\ell} =\frac{\ell M'(\ell)}{M(\ell)}. $$ Ordinary diffusion has $M=2D\ell$ and $\alpha=1$. A roughly constant velocity over a short interval gives displacement $v\ell$ and $M=\mathbb E[v^2]\ell^2$, so $\alpha=2$. [Growth faster than linear is called [**superdiffusion**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}. Here it describes a finite range of lags. It does not assert a single power law for arbitrarily long times.]{.definition-explanation}[^p2-msd-result] Could temporally uncorrelated motor noise acquire the observed MSD just by passing through muscles? [A [**low pass filter**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} suppresses rapid input changes relative to slow ones.]{.definition-explanation} [[**White noise**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} here is an ideal zero mean input whose fluctuations at different times are uncorrelated. In continuous time its strength is defined by an intensity multiplying a delta function, rather than a finite variance at an individual time.]{.definition-explanation} [A stable, decaying response to this noise produces a [**stationary process**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} in the sense needed here: its mean is constant and its covariance depends only on time separation.]{.definition-explanation} Its position variance consequently does not grow with absolute time. Let $E=h*\xi$, where $$ \mathbb E[\xi(t)\xi(t')]=A\delta(t-t'). $$ The noise intensity $A$ has units input$^2$ times seconds. Expanding the convolution and using the delta function yields, for $\ell\ge0$, $$ C_E(\ell)=\mathbb E[E(t)E(t+\ell)] =A\int_0^\infty h(u)h(u+\ell)\,du. $$ For a stationary centered position, expanding the squared difference then gives $$ M(\ell)=2[C_E(0)-C_E(\ell)]. $$ If the kernel decays sufficiently rapidly, its overlap with a shifted copy tends to zero. The MSD consequently approaches $2C_E(0)$, a finite plateau. This reconstructs the reasoning of Eqs. 20–22.[^p2-white-noise] For the one exponential filter $h(u)=\Theta(u)e^{-u/\tau}/\tau$, $$ C_E(\ell)=\frac{A}{2\tau}e^{-\ell/\tau},\qquad M_{\rm white}(\ell)=\frac A\tau(1-e^{-\ell/\tau}). $$ This simple filter has a short lag MSD proportional to $\ell$ and a long lag plateau. A double exponential filter is smoother at short lags, but still gives a plateau because its kernel also decays. Increasing $A$ raises the curve without removing its flattening. The paper's simulated private OMN noise, passed through muscle dynamics, is both too small and too flat at long lags. In Fig. 3b, using 2,000 heterogeneous OMNs, its contribution is about 1% of the observed variance near 900 ms.[^p2-msd-result]
Original paper figure: Ben-Shushan et al. (2022), Figure 3
{{block:fig:PAPER-EYE-3}}
Filtered white noise cannot explain continued long-lag growth. Suppose instead the input is a stored position $B(t)$ undergoing Brownian motion with $\mathbb E[(B(t+\ell)-B(t))^2]=2D\ell$. Its position variance accumulates. A low pass filter with nonzero static gain smooths the path while retaining that accumulating long time displacement variance. The following one exponential example is a teaching reconstruction, not the paper's full muscle model. It derives how smooth movement can have a slope between one and two even though the stored position undergoes ordinary diffusion. Let $$ \tau\dot E+E=B,\qquad dB=\sqrt{2D}\,dW. $$ Here $B$ is the changing position command and $E$ is the eye angle that follows it, both in degrees. The mismatch $B-E$ drives velocity: a command to the right of the current position makes the eye move right. For the same mismatch, a larger response time $\tau$ gives a smaller velocity, so the eye takes longer to catch up and smooths rapid command changes more strongly. This response time belongs to the simplified eye filter. It is not automatically the synaptic decay time used in the memory model. $W$ is a Brownian process with unit increment variance per unit time, so $D$ has units deg$^2$/s. Define velocity $v=\dot E=(B-E)/\tau$. Taking its increment gives $$ \tau\,dv=-v\,dt+\sqrt{2D}\,dW. $$ Velocity loses its past value over time $\tau$ and receives new random input. To add the surviving effect of those inputs, divide the past into short intervals of width $h$. The Brownian change $\Delta W_j=W(u_j+h)-W(u_j)$ has mean zero and variance $h$. Changes in disjoint intervals are independent. Its contribution to the velocity at time $t$ is approximately $(\sqrt{2D}/\tau)e^{-(t-u_j)/\tau}\Delta W_j$: the initial change has decayed between $u_j$ and $t$. The integral against $dW(u)$ denotes the limit of these weighted sums as $h$ tends to zero. It does not require an ordinary derivative of the Brownian path. After the initial velocity has decayed, extending the input history into the distant past gives $$ v(t)=\frac{\sqrt{2D}}{\tau}\int_{-\infty}^{t}e^{-(t-u)/\tau}\,dW(u). $$ For a lag $s\geq0$, multiply the sums for $v(t)$ and $v(t+s)$ and average. Products of distinct increments have zero mean. The same increment contributes its variance $h$, so the sum becomes an ordinary overlap integral over their shared past: $$ \begin{aligned} C_v(s) &=\frac{2D}{\tau^2}\int_{-\infty}^{t} e^{-(t-u)/\tau}e^{-(t+s-u)/\tau}\,du\\ &=\frac{2D}{\tau^2}e^{-s/\tau}\int_0^\infty e^{-2r/\tau}\,dr =\frac D\tau e^{-s/\tau}. \end{aligned} $$ Here $r=t-u$ is the age of an input increment. Covariance is even in the lag, so $C_v(s)=(D/\tau)e^{-|s|/\tau}$ for either sign of $s$. Integrating velocity over an interval gives position change. The double integral over its covariance reduces to $$ \begin{aligned} M_{\rm Brownian}(\ell) &=\int_0^\ell\int_0^\ell C_v(u-v)\,du\,dv\\ &=2\int_0^\ell(\ell-s)C_v(s)\,ds\\ &=2D[\ell-\tau(1-e^{-\ell/\tau})]. \end{aligned} $$ At short lags, $1-e^{-\ell/\tau}=\ell/\tau-\ell^2/(2\tau^2)+\cdots$, so $$ M_{\rm Brownian}(\ell)\simeq(D/\tau)\ell^2. $$ The eye keeps approximately the same velocity over that interval. At long lags, $$ M_{\rm Brownian}(\ell)\simeq2D(\ell-\tau), $$ which grows linearly rather than approaching a plateau. Holding the internal diffusion coefficient $D$ fixed, increasing $\tau$ reduces short-lag displacement and moves the transition to linear growth to longer lags. It does not stop accumulating error: the long-lag MSD growth rate still approaches $2D$. Increasing $D$ instead raises the entire MSD curve in proportion, at fixed $\tau$. The local logarithmic slope of this MSD is $$ \alpha(\ell)=\frac{\ell(1-e^{-\ell/\tau})} {\ell-\tau(1-e^{-\ell/\tau})}, $$ approaching two at short lags and one at long lags. At $\ell=\tau$ it is $e-1\simeq1.718$. At $\ell=5\tau$ it is about $1.239$. [Thus an intermediate slope can arise from filtering ordinary diffusion, without faster than Brownian accumulation inside the memory circuit.]{.key-statement} The curves compare the two inputs after the same filter with one exponential response, also called a one pole filter.
{{block:fig:EYE-FILTERED-NOISE-MSD}}
The white-input short-lag slope of one belongs to this one-pole example. The actual muscle response contains fast and slow exponential components, and the full model also contains motor neuron filtering and feedback. Those ingredients change the detailed curve. The one exponential derivation teaches the distinction relevant to Fig. 3: [a decaying low pass filter of stationary white noise saturates, whereas the same filter, with nonzero static gain, retains accumulating displacement from a wandering position. review_metadata.title: Drift growth distinguishes diffusion from filtered white noise
review_metadata.purpose: Eye movements recorded during steady gaze in monkeys look different over short and long time intervals. This chapter uses their timing to distinguish fluctuations around a fixed command from accumulated changes in the command, while accounting for eye-position measurement error.

review_metadata.title: A noisy memory circuit can produce eye drift
review_metadata.purpose: A circuit that stores the intended eye angle is one possible source of fixational drift. This chapter follows the proposed model from interacting neurons through motor neurons and muscles to eye motion, and explains how delayed visual feedback can limit that motion.
