# A noisy memory circuit can produce eye drift {#ch:EYE-CIRCUIT} The recordings support a shared source before the motor neurons, and the movement's timing is compatible with a stored position that wanders. [Neither result identifies the circuit that supplies that command. A noisy memory circuit is a proposed explanation whose output must pass through the motor neurons and muscles before it can be compared with eye movement.]{.key-statement} Following that complete path lets the model test whether neural noise can produce both the amount and timing of the observed drift. Its spike variability, neuron count and time constants determine how much freedom this match allows. Comparing the model with the separate recording and timing results then shows what the study supports, and why it still leaves other upstream sources possible. ## A noisy integrator can reproduce drift after muscle filtering {#sec:EYE-CIRCUIT-MODEL} The recording analysis places much of the drive upstream of OMNs. To test whether integrator noise could supply it, the authors build a model from a noisy memory circuit through to the eye. The model adapts an earlier goldfish integrator architecture to primate tuning and variability. The model has two groups of integrator neurons. One group fires more when the eye points farther right. The other fires more when it points farther left. Neurons excite cells in their own group and inhibit cells in the other group. The connection strengths are tuned so that the circuit can approximately maintain a range of represented eye positions.[^p2-network] For the right population, the model's rate is $$ \lambda_i^R(t)=\left[\zeta_i^R E_{OI}(t)+\lambda_i^0+\zeta_i^R F(t)\right]_+, \qquad [a]_+=\max(a,0). $$ $E_{OI}$ is the internally represented position in degrees, $\zeta_i^R$ is a tuning slope in spikes/(s deg), and $\lambda_i^0$ is a rate offset in spikes/s. Taking the maximum with zero prevents negative firing. $F$ is a feedback input in degrees, defined below. The matching left neuron has the opposite slope, $\zeta_i^L=-\zeta_i^R$. In an active neuron, a change of one degree changes its rate by $\zeta_i$. The model scales each spike train into an input $X_i$ with a saturating mean response. This input changes the neuron's synaptic output $S_i$, the lingering effect of its spikes on neurons receiving them. A weighted difference between the two groups' synaptic outputs gives the represented eye angle $E_{OI}$. This value sets the firing rates again, closing the feedback loop: $$ \tau_s\dot S_i^R=-S_i^R+X_i^R,\qquad X_i^R(t)=\frac{\xi_i^R(t)}{\lambda_t+\lambda_i^R(t)},\qquad E_{OI}(t)=\sum_i\eta_i[S_i^R(t)-S_i^L(t)]. $$ Here $\xi_i^R$ is a spike train generated at rate $\lambda_i^R$, $\tau_s$ is the synaptic decay time, and $\lambda_t=60$ Hz sets the rate scale in the nonlinear synaptic response. Treating spikes as counts, $X_i$ and $S_i$ are dimensionless, and the weights $\eta_i$ are in degrees. Between spikes, $S_i$ decays exponentially. One spike adds a jump of $1/[\tau_s(\lambda_t+\lambda_i^R)]$. Replacing spikes by their mean rate gives a drive $\lambda_i^R/(\lambda_t+\lambda_i^R)$ that approaches one as the rate increases. This is the model's saturating synaptic effect, rather than the purely linear synapses of the basic 2012 example.[^p2-network] Persistence requires a further condition on that feedback. Set $F=0$ and replace spikes by their mean rates. Define the mean saturated drives at a proposed stored value $z$ by $$ q_i^R(z)=\frac{\lambda_i^R(z)}{\lambda_t+\lambda_i^R(z)}, \qquad q_i^L(z)=\frac{\lambda_i^L(z)}{\lambda_t+\lambda_i^L(z)}. $$ Multiply each synaptic equation by its readout weight, subtract the left contribution, and sum. Since the same $\tau_s$ applies to every unit, the readout obeys $$ \tau_s\dot E_{OI}=-E_{OI}+G(E_{OI}), \qquad G(z)=\sum_i\eta_i[q_i^R(z)-q_i^L(z)]. $$ [An exact continuum of persistent readout values would require $G(z)=z$ over the represented range.]{.key-statement} For a small displacement from a fixed value, Taylor expansion gives $$ \tau_s\,\frac{d\,\delta E_{OI}}{dt} =[G'(z)-1]\delta E_{OI}. $$ Thus $G'(z)=1$ is the local neutral condition for the stored coordinate. Stable directions of the remaining synaptic state are also needed for an attractor. The weights were optimized to approximate the fixed-point relation across $-50$ to $50$ degrees. [Residual mismatch can produce deterministic drift, so this finite optimized circuit provides approximate persistence rather than an exactly neutral continuum.]{.key-statement} The tuning slopes and thresholds were sampled to match reported macaque relationships and variation. With spikes, perturbations along the nearly neutral direction also accumulate. This reduction is a teaching derivation from the paper's equations. Figure 4 separates the resulting internal diffusion from later muscle smoothing.[^p2-network]
Original paper figure: Ben-Shushan et al. (2022), Figure 4
{{block:fig:PAPER-EYE-4}}
The motor neurons receive this position signal: $$ \lambda_i^M(t)=[k_i(E_{OI}(t)-E_{T_i})]_+, \qquad \tau_{MN}\dot s_i^M=-s_i^M+\xi_i^M. $$ $\lambda_i^M$ is a motor rate in spikes/s, $E_{T_i}$ is that neuron's position threshold in degrees, and $k_i$ is its position sensitivity. $\xi_i^M$ is its generated spike train. The filtered output $s_i^M$ also has units spikes/s, with decay time $\tau_{MN}$. One spike makes a jump of $1/\tau_{MN}$. At constant mean rate, the mean output is that rate. Each motor unit's muscle and plant response is represented by a position contribution $E_i$ satisfying $$ s_i^M=k_i(E_i-E_{T_i})+r_i\dot E_i+m_i\ddot E_i, \qquad E=\frac1{N_m}\sum_{i=1}^{N_m}E_i. $$ These are Eqs. 28–31. The second order equation uses the same roles and units as the forward fit. At constant $E_{OI}$, an active unit has mean $s_i^M=k_i(E_{OI}-E_{T_i})$, giving mean $E_i=E_{OI}$ when derivatives vanish. Averaging therefore transmits the common position while reducing independent private fluctuations. This is an effective model of combined motor output, not a claim that one motor unit moves an isolated eye of its own.[^p2-motor] The model used diverse thresholds and response coefficients, with motor thresholds sampled between $-45$ and $-5$ degrees, and imposed $m_i The effect on the ongoing MSD must be checked from the coupled model, rather than inferred from the delay alone. A short MSD lag is a separation between two samples in a running process, not the time since a new perturbation. Past measurements can already affect both samples, and $F$ also contains the immediate term $-A E_{OI}(t)$. Extended Data Fig. 3 compares the model with and without feedback: feedback changes amplitude across lags, while its larger effect on logarithmic slope occurs at longer lags. Figure 5 shows the full model. [Muscle filtering supplies the short-lag smoothness, and feedback improves the detailed longer-lag fit. These are results of this model comparison, not a hard delay-based cutoff or a claim excluding visual control under other tasks.]{.key-statement}[^p2-feedback]
Original paper figure: Ben-Shushan et al. (2022), Figure 5
{{block:fig:PAPER-EYE-5}}
Original paper figure: Ben-Shushan et al. (2022), Extended Data Figure 3
{{block:fig:PAPER-EYE-ED3}}
## Spike regularity and circuit parameters set the model's drift scale {#sec:EYE-SCALING} An agreement in amplitude is informative only if we know how much freedom the model has. The paper uses regular spike trains. The [spike variability section](ch-foundations.html#sec-foundations-poisson) defined the interspike interval coefficient of variation (CV) as the interval standard deviation divided by its mean. A Poisson process at constant rate has CV one. The model uses about 0.22 for integrator neurons and about 0.07 for OMNs. [Such firing is called [**sub-Poisson spiking**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} here because its long window count variability is lower than a Poisson process at the same rate, under the interval construction used in the model.]{.definition-explanation}[^p2-cv] The construction starts with a Poisson process at $M$ times the desired rate and retains every $M$th spike. At constant rate, a retained interval is the sum of $M$ independent exponential intervals. Each initial interval has mean $1/(M\lambda)$ and variance $1/(M\lambda)^2$. The retained interval therefore has mean $1/\lambda$, variance $1/(M\lambda^2)$, and CV $1/\sqrt M$. This preserves the mean rate while reducing variability. Its use at changing rates is part of the model. The simple interval derivation assumes a constant rate. At constant rate, the retained intervals are independent. [This is a [**renewal process**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}, a spike process whose successive intervals are independent and identically distributed.]{.definition-explanation} Let their mean be $\mu=1/\lambda$ and standard deviation $\sigma_I$. The time to $n$ spikes has variance $n\sigma_I^2$. For a long fixed window $L\simeq n\mu$, a fluctuation in total interval time produces the opposite fluctuation in count divided by $\mu$. Thus $$ \operatorname{Var}(n)\simeq\frac{n\sigma_I^2}{\mu^2} \simeq\lambda L\left(\frac{\sigma_I}{\mu}\right)^2 =\lambda L\,\mathrm{CV}^2. $$ This explains why the diffusion scale contains CV squared: it is the strength of the accumulated spike fluctuations relative to the Poisson case. The [diffusion calculation](ch-memory-dynamics.html#sec-memory-diffusion) and [information bound](ch-memory-information.html#sec-memory-bound) show how projecting those fluctuations onto a neutral memory direction adds a factor proportional to $1/\tau_s^2$ and, for a comparable independent population, $1/N$. Rate and sensitivity need more care. Write the absolute local rate slope as $a=d\lambda/dE$, in spikes/(s deg). If $N$ similar cells fire near rate $\lambda_0$, their Poisson information per unit time about position is $$ J\simeq\frac{Na^2}{\lambda_0}. $$ Using the [information-diffusion relation](ch-memory-information.html#sec-memory-bound) as a scale, including the $\mathrm{CV}^2$ factor just derived and holding the network geometry fixed, $$ D\ \propto\ \frac{\mathrm{CV}^2}{\tau_s^2J} =\frac{\mathrm{CV}^2\lambda_0}{N a^2\tau_s^2}. $$ If instead sensitivity is expressed as the fractional slope $b=a/\lambda_0$, in inverse degrees, the same expression becomes $$ D\ \propto\ \frac{\mathrm{CV}^2}{N\lambda_0 b^2\tau_s^2}. $$ This second form has the dependence printed in the paper's Eq. 1, $D\propto\mathrm{CV}^2N^{-1}\lambda_0^{-1}k_0^{-2}\tau_s^{-2}$. However, its surrounding text calls $k_0$ position sensitivity without specifying fractional normalization. If $k_0$ means an absolute slope in Hz/degree, that printed expression has the wrong units for $D$. The version with $\lambda_0$ in the numerator has the required units deg$^2$/s. This scaling is a comparison under fixed network geometry and noise assumptions, not an exact formula for every recurrent circuit.[^p2-scaling] At fixed network geometry and under the noise assumptions above, the scale changes as follows: - Doubling $N$ halves it. - Doubling CV multiplies it by four. - Doubling $\tau_s$ divides it by four. - Doubling the absolute slope at fixed rate also divides it by four. [Increasing rate reduces diffusion when the fractional slope is fixed, because more spikes then also supply a proportionally steeper absolute slope. Increasing rate at fixed absolute slope is a different comparison and increases the scale in the first formula. A rate change alone does not specify which comparison is intended.]{.key-statement} Could the measured CV itself mostly reflect drift rather than private spike variability? Supplementary Notes test this. Let $\lambda(t)=\bar\lambda+aB(t)$ during a fixation of length $T$, with the rate changes small relative to $\bar\lambda$. For a Brownian path starting at zero, the expected time averaged squared position is $DT$, and the expected squared time mean is $2DT/3$. Subtracting gives the expected within-segment position variance $DT/3=2DT/6$: $$ \mathbb E\!\left[\frac1T\int_0^T(B(t)-\bar B)^2dt\right] =\frac{DT}{3}. $$ The second term follows from $\mathbb E[B(t)B(s)]=2D\min(t,s)$ and $T^{-2}\int_0^T\int_0^T2D\min(t,s)\,dt\,ds=2DT/3$. Expanding $1/(\bar\lambda+aB)$ to first order gives $1/\bar\lambda-aB/\bar\lambda^2$. Dividing its standard deviation by its mean then gives $$ \mathrm{CV}_{\rm drift}\simeq \frac{|a|}{\bar\lambda}\sqrt{\frac{2DT}{6}}. $$ With the supplement's values $a=1/15$ spikes/(s arcmin), $2D=100$ arcmin$^2$/s, $T=0.5$ s, and $\bar\lambda=80$ Hz, this is about $0.0024$, well below the OMN CV near 0.07. These are an order of magnitude check, not a fitted diffusion constant for the whole model. Since one degree is 60 arcmin, that $2D$ equals $0.0278$ deg$^2$/s, or $D=0.0139$ deg$^2$/s.[^p2-cv-drift] ## The figures test shared drive, diffusion, and the full circuit model {#sec:EYE-FIGURES} The five figures address different steps. Their agreement is easier to assess when those questions remain separate.
{{block:tbl:EYE-FIGURE-GUIDE}}
The most useful supplemental comparisons are Extended Data Fig. 1 for individual uncertainty, Fig. 2 for noise subtraction and its simulated control, Fig. 3 for feedback, Fig. 4 for a no-central-drive control, and Fig. 5 for the other monkey's fit. In the no-central-drive control, $\widehat\chi=-0.09\pm0.22$ is compatible with zero. That negative estimate is sampling variation. Figures 6–8 document cell classification, segment sampling, and a rank correlation check. Figure 9 shows the heterogeneous model parameters. Figure 10 separates spiking noise passed directly to the output from spiking noise that drives diffusion inside the integrator: internal stochastic spikes remain in the latter comparison. Its caption reports little direct output-noise effect beyond 50 ms.[^p2-supp-figures]

## The evidence places shared drive upstream without identifying one circuit {#sec:EYE-LIMITS} The data and model answer different questions about where the drive originates: - The common variance estimate supports a drive upstream of OMNs, given the calibration and noise assumptions. - The MSD comparison supports a command that accumulates variation over the measured interval, rather than stationary white noise passed through a decaying muscle filter. - The circuit model shows that integrator noise with plausible parameters can generate such a command and explain its filtered amplitude and timing. Those results do not uniquely locate the noise inside integrator neurons. Two missing tests limit that conclusion: - No integrator neurons were recorded in this study. - No selective change of that circuit tested whether it was necessary for drift. [Noisy inputs to the integrator, or an already diffusive upstream signal, remain possible. The authors make this distinction in the Discussion and explicitly in their peer review response. Several combinations of neuron count, variability, and synaptic time constant can also fit an amplitude, so matching one curve does not uniquely recover those parameters.]{.key-statement}[^p2-localization] The study's empirical scope is horizontal motion during these fixation segments in two animals. Visual tasks, feedback, and other sources of input can alter the statistics. Its contribution to the connection with the 2012 theory is more precise: a continuous memory can diffuse internally, while a mechanical output of that memory looks smooth and superdiffusive at shorter lags. To compare a memory theory with behavior, the mapping from stored value to measured movement is part of the calculation. [^p2-network]: Ben-Shushan, N., Shaham, N., Joshua, M., & Burak, Y. (2022). *Fixational drift is driven by diffusive dynamics in central neural circuitry*. Nature Communications, 13, 1697. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-022-29201-y). (2022). *Fixational drift is driven by diffusive dynamics in central neural circuitry*. Nature Communications, 13, 1697. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-022-29201-y). Main p. 11, “OMN activity and actual eye position,” Eqs. 28–33 and simulation parameters; p. 6, Fig. 3 caption, private OMN comparison. [^p2-feedback]: Ben-Shushan, N., Shaham, N., Joshua, M., & Burak, Y. (2022). *Fixational drift is driven by diffusive dynamics in central neural circuitry*. Nature Communications, 13, 1697. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-022-29201-y). Main pp. 7, 9, 11, “Visual feedback,” Eq. 34; Supplementary Information, pp. 4–5 and p. 9, Extended Data Fig. 3. Some supplement cross references use earlier figure/equation numbers. Page 5 also mentions 15K integrator neurons, whereas final main Methods specify 30,000. This guide uses final main paper numbering and its main simulation parameters. [^p2-cv]: Ben-Shushan, N., Shaham, N., Joshua, M., & Burak, Y. (2022). *Fixational drift is driven by diffusive dynamics in central neural circuitry*. Nature Communications, 13, 1697. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-022-29201-y). Main p. 11, “Sub-Poisson spike trains,” Eq. 35 and integrator variability specification. The interval-sum derivation expands the construction given there. [^p2-scaling]: Ben-Shushan, N., Shaham, N., Joshua, M., & Burak, Y. (2022). *Fixational drift is driven by diffusive dynamics in central neural circuitry*. Nature Communications, 13, 1697. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-022-29201-y). Main p. 6, Eq. 1 and its parameter discussion; peer review file, p. 23, changes in slope, synaptic time constant, and neuron count. The absolute versus fractional slope distinction is the guide's dimensional interpretation of the printed normalization ambiguity, connected to the guide’s diffusion and information calculations. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-022-29201-y). Supplementary Information, pp. 2–3, “Contribution of oculomotor state to the CV of OMNs,” Eqs. S3–S6. ## The evidence places shared drive upstream without identifying one circuit {#sec:EYE-LIMITS}

The data and model answer different questions about where the drive originates:

- The common variance estimate supports a drive upstream of OMNs, given the calibration and noise assumptions.
- The MSD comparison supports a command that accumulates variation over the measured interval, rather than stationary white noise passed through a decaying muscle filter.
- The circuit model shows that integrator noise with plausible parameters can generate such a command and explain its filtered amplitude and timing.

<!-- vale ai-tells.CataphoricForecasting = NO -->
Those results do not uniquely locate the noise inside integrator neurons. Two missing tests limit that conclusion:
<!-- vale ai-tells.CataphoricForecasting = YES -->

  <!-- vale ai-tells.NegatedSubject = NO -->
- No integrator neurons were recorded in this study.
  <!-- vale ai-tells.NegatedSubject = YES -->
- No selective change of that circuit tested whether it was necessary for drift.

[Noisy inputs to the integrator, or an already diffusive upstream signal, remain possible. The authors make this distinction in the Discussion and explicitly in their peer review response. Several combinations of neuron count, variability, and synaptic time constant can also fit an amplitude, so matching one curve does not uniquely recover those parameters.]{.key-statement}[^p2-localization]

<!-- vale ai-tells.ServesAsDodge = NO -->
The study's empirical scope is horizontal motion during these fixation segments in two animals. Visual tasks, feedback, and other sources of input can alter the statistics. Its contribution to the connection with the 2012 theory is more precise: a continuous memory can diffuse internally, while a mechanical output of that memory looks smooth and superdiffusive at shorter lags. To compare a memory theory with behavior, the mapping from stored value to measured movement is part of the calculation.

review_metadata.title: A noisy memory circuit can produce eye drift
review_metadata.purpose: A circuit that stores the intended eye angle is one possible source of fixational drift. This chapter follows the proposed model from interacting neurons through motor neurons and muscles to eye motion, and explains how delayed visual feedback can limit that motion.

section_list.title: A noisy integrator can reproduce drift after muscle filtering
section_list.summary: The recording analysis places much of the drive upstream of OMNs. To test whether integrator noise could supply it, the authors build a model from a noisy memory circuit through to the eye. The model adapts an earlier goldfish integrator architecture to primate tuning and variability. The model has two groups of integrator neurons. One group fires more when the eye points farther right. The other fires more when it points farther left. Neurons excite cells in their own group and inhibit cells in the other group. The connection strengths are tuned so that the circuit can approximately maintain a range of represented eye positions.[^p2-network]

section_list.title: Spike regularity and circuit parameters set the model's drift scale
section_list.summary: An agreement in amplitude is informative only if we know how much freedom the model has. The paper uses regular spike trains. The [spike variability section](ch-foundations.html#sec-foundations-poisson) defined the interspike interval coefficient of variation (CV) as the interval standard deviation divided by its mean. A Poisson process at constant rate has CV one. The model uses about 0.22 for integrator neurons and about 0.07 for OMNs. Such firing is called [**sub-Poisson spiking**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} here because its long window count variability is lower than a Poisson process at the same rate, under the interval construction used in the model.[^p2-cv]

section_list.summary: The five figures address different steps. Their agreement is easier to assess when those questions remain separate.

content/chapters/04c-eye-circuit.md::sec.review_asset_definitions:
# A noisy memory circuit can produce eye drift {#ch:EYE-CIRCUIT} The recordings support a shared source before the motor neurons, and the movement's timing is compatible with a stored position that wanders. [Neither result identifies the circuit that supplies that command. A noisy memory circuit is a proposed explanation whose output must pass through the motor neurons and muscles before it can be compared with eye movement.]{.key-statement} Following that complete path lets the model test whether neural noise can produce both the amount and timing of the observed drift. Its spike variability, neuron count and time constants determine how much freedom this match allows. Comparing the model with the separate recording and timing results then shows what the study supports, and why it still leaves other upstream sources possible. ## A noisy integrator can reproduce drift after muscle filtering {#sec:EYE-CIRCUIT-MODEL} The recording analysis places much of the drive upstream of OMNs. To test whether integrator noise could supply it, the authors build a model from a noisy memory circuit through to the eye. The model adapts an earlier goldfish integrator architecture to primate tuning and variability. The model has two groups of integrator neurons. One group fires more when the eye points farther right. The other fires more when it points farther left. Neurons excite cells in their own group and inhibit cells in the other group. The connection strengths are tuned so that the circuit can approximately maintain a range of represented eye positions.[^p2-network] For the right population, the model's rate is $$ \lambda_i^R(t)=\left[\zeta_i^R E_{OI}(t)+\lambda_i^0+\zeta_i^R F(t)\right]_+, \qquad [a]_+=\max(a,0). $$ $E_{OI}$ is the internally represented position in degrees, $\zeta_i^R$ is a tuning slope in spikes/(s deg), and $\lambda_i^0$ is a rate offset in spikes/s. Taking the maximum with zero prevents negative firing. $F$ is a feedback input in degrees, defined below. The matching left neuron has the opposite slope, $\zeta_i^L=-\zeta_i^R$. In an active neuron, a change of one degree changes its rate by $\zeta_i$. The model scales each spike train into an input $X_i$ with a saturating mean response. This input changes the neuron's synaptic output $S_i$, the lingering effect of its spikes on neurons receiving them. A weighted difference between the two groups' synaptic outputs gives the represented eye angle $E_{OI}$. This value sets the firing rates again, closing the feedback loop: $$ \tau_s\dot S_i^R=-S_i^R+X_i^R,\qquad X_i^R(t)=\frac{\xi_i^R(t)}{\lambda_t+\lambda_i^R(t)},\qquad E_{OI}(t)=\sum_i\eta_i[S_i^R(t)-S_i^L(t)]. $$ Here $\xi_i^R$ is a spike train generated at rate $\lambda_i^R$, $\tau_s$ is the synaptic decay time, and $\lambda_t=60$ Hz sets the rate scale in the nonlinear synaptic response. Treating spikes as counts, $X_i$ and $S_i$ are dimensionless, and the weights $\eta_i$ are in degrees. Between spikes, $S_i$ decays exponentially. One spike adds a jump of $1/[\tau_s(\lambda_t+\lambda_i^R)]$. Replacing spikes by their mean rate gives a drive $\lambda_i^R/(\lambda_t+\lambda_i^R)$ that approaches one as the rate increases. This is the model's saturating synaptic effect, rather than the purely linear synapses of the basic 2012 example.[^p2-network] Persistence requires a further condition on that feedback. Set $F=0$ and replace spikes by their mean rates. Define the mean saturated drives at a proposed stored value $z$ by $$ q_i^R(z)=\frac{\lambda_i^R(z)}{\lambda_t+\lambda_i^R(z)}, \qquad q_i^L(z)=\frac{\lambda_i^L(z)}{\lambda_t+\lambda_i^L(z)}. $$ Multiply each synaptic equation by its readout weight, subtract the left contribution, and sum. Since the same $\tau_s$ applies to every unit, the readout obeys $$ \tau_s\dot E_{OI}=-E_{OI}+G(E_{OI}), \qquad G(z)=\sum_i\eta_i[q_i^R(z)-q_i^L(z)]. $$ [An exact continuum of persistent readout values would require $G(z)=z$ over the represented range.]{.key-statement} For a small displacement from a fixed value, Taylor expansion gives $$ \tau_s\,\frac{d\,\delta E_{OI}}{dt} =[G'(z)-1]\delta E_{OI}. $$ Thus $G'(z)=1$ is the local neutral condition for the stored coordinate. Stable directions of the remaining synaptic state are also needed for an attractor. The weights were optimized to approximate the fixed-point relation across $-50$ to $50$ degrees. [Residual mismatch can produce deterministic drift, so this finite optimized circuit provides approximate persistence rather than an exactly neutral continuum.]{.key-statement} The tuning slopes and thresholds were sampled to match reported macaque relationships and variation. With spikes, perturbations along the nearly neutral direction also accumulate. This reduction is a teaching derivation from the paper's equations. Figure 4 separates the resulting internal diffusion from later muscle smoothing.[^p2-network]
Original paper figure: Ben-Shushan et al. (2022), Figure 4
{{block:fig:PAPER-EYE-4}}
The motor neurons receive this position signal: $$ \lambda_i^M(t)=[k_i(E_{OI}(t)-E_{T_i})]_+, \qquad \tau_{MN}\dot s_i^M=-s_i^M+\xi_i^M. $$ $\lambda_i^M$ is a motor rate in spikes/s, $E_{T_i}$ is that neuron's position threshold in degrees, and $k_i$ is its position sensitivity. $\xi_i^M$ is its generated spike train. The filtered output $s_i^M$ also has units spikes/s, with decay time $\tau_{MN}$. One spike makes a jump of $1/\tau_{MN}$. At constant mean rate, the mean output is that rate. Each motor unit's muscle and plant response is represented by a position contribution $E_i$ satisfying $$ s_i^M=k_i(E_i-E_{T_i})+r_i\dot E_i+m_i\ddot E_i, \qquad E=\frac1{N_m}\sum_{i=1}^{N_m}E_i. $$ These are Eqs. 28–31. The second order equation uses the same roles and units as the forward fit. At constant $E_{OI}$, an active unit has mean $s_i^M=k_i(E_{OI}-E_{T_i})$, giving mean $E_i=E_{OI}$ when derivatives vanish. Averaging therefore transmits the common position while reducing independent private fluctuations. This is an effective model of combined motor output, not a claim that one motor unit moves an isolated eye of its own.[^p2-motor] The model used diverse thresholds and response coefficients, with motor thresholds sampled between $-45$ and $-5$ degrees, and imposed $m_i The effect on the ongoing MSD must be checked from the coupled model, rather than inferred from the delay alone. A short MSD lag is a separation between two samples in a running process, not the time since a new perturbation. Past measurements can already affect both samples, and $F$ also contains the immediate term $-A E_{OI}(t)$. Extended Data Fig. 3 compares the model with and without feedback: feedback changes amplitude across lags, while its larger effect on logarithmic slope occurs at longer lags. Figure 5 shows the full model. [Muscle filtering supplies the short-lag smoothness, and feedback improves the detailed longer-lag fit. These are results of this model comparison, not a hard delay-based cutoff or a claim excluding visual control under other tasks.]{.key-statement}[^p2-feedback]
Original paper figure: Ben-Shushan et al. (2022), Figure 5
{{block:fig:PAPER-EYE-5}}
Original paper figure: Ben-Shushan et al. (2022), Extended Data Figure 3
{{block:fig:PAPER-EYE-ED3}}
## Spike regularity and circuit parameters set the model's drift scale {#sec:EYE-SCALING} An agreement in amplitude is informative only if we know how much freedom the model has. The paper uses regular spike trains. The [spike variability section](ch-foundations.html#sec-foundations-poisson) defined the interspike interval coefficient of variation (CV) as the interval standard deviation divided by its mean. A Poisson process at constant rate has CV one. The model uses about 0.22 for integrator neurons and about 0.07 for OMNs. [Such firing is called [**sub-Poisson spiking**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} here because its long window count variability is lower than a Poisson process at the same rate, under the interval construction used in the model.]{.definition-explanation}[^p2-cv] The construction starts with a Poisson process at $M$ times the desired rate and retains every $M$th spike. At constant rate, a retained interval is the sum of $M$ independent exponential intervals. Each initial interval has mean $1/(M\lambda)$ and variance $1/(M\lambda)^2$. The retained interval therefore has mean $1/\lambda$, variance $1/(M\lambda^2)$, and CV $1/\sqrt M$. This preserves the mean rate while reducing variability. Its use at changing rates is part of the model. The simple interval derivation assumes a constant rate. At constant rate, the retained intervals are independent. [This is a [**renewal process**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}, a spike process whose successive intervals are independent and identically distributed.]{.definition-explanation} Let their mean be $\mu=1/\lambda$ and standard deviation $\sigma_I$. The time to $n$ spikes has variance $n\sigma_I^2$. For a long fixed window $L\simeq n\mu$, a fluctuation in total interval time produces the opposite fluctuation in count divided by $\mu$. Thus $$ \operatorname{Var}(n)\simeq\frac{n\sigma_I^2}{\mu^2} \simeq\lambda L\left(\frac{\sigma_I}{\mu}\right)^2 =\lambda L\,\mathrm{CV}^2. $$ This explains why the diffusion scale contains CV squared: it is the strength of the accumulated spike fluctuations relative to the Poisson case. The [diffusion calculation](ch-memory-dynamics.html#sec-memory-diffusion) and [information bound](ch-memory-information.html#sec-memory-bound) show how projecting those fluctuations onto a neutral memory direction adds a factor proportional to $1/\tau_s^2$ and, for a comparable independent population, $1/N$. Rate and sensitivity need more care. Write the absolute local rate slope as $a=d\lambda/dE$, in spikes/(s deg). If $N$ similar cells fire near rate $\lambda_0$, their Poisson information per unit time about position is $$ J\simeq\frac{Na^2}{\lambda_0}. $$ Using the [information-diffusion relation](ch-memory-information.html#sec-memory-bound) as a scale, including the $\mathrm{CV}^2$ factor just derived and holding the network geometry fixed, $$ D\ \propto\ \frac{\mathrm{CV}^2}{\tau_s^2J} =\frac{\mathrm{CV}^2\lambda_0}{N a^2\tau_s^2}. $$ If instead sensitivity is expressed as the fractional slope $b=a/\lambda_0$, in inverse degrees, the same expression becomes $$ D\ \propto\ \frac{\mathrm{CV}^2}{N\lambda_0 b^2\tau_s^2}. $$ This second form has the dependence printed in the paper's Eq. 1, $D\propto\mathrm{CV}^2N^{-1}\lambda_0^{-1}k_0^{-2}\tau_s^{-2}$. However, its surrounding text calls $k_0$ position sensitivity without specifying fractional normalization. If $k_0$ means an absolute slope in Hz/degree, that printed expression has the wrong units for $D$. The version with $\lambda_0$ in the numerator has the required units deg$^2$/s. This scaling is a comparison under fixed network geometry and noise assumptions, not an exact formula for every recurrent circuit.[^p2-scaling] At fixed network geometry and under the noise assumptions above, the scale changes as follows: - Doubling $N$ halves it. - Doubling CV multiplies it by four. - Doubling $\tau_s$ divides it by four. - Doubling the absolute slope at fixed rate also divides it by four. [Increasing rate reduces diffusion when the fractional slope is fixed, because more spikes then also supply a proportionally steeper absolute slope. Increasing rate at fixed absolute slope is a different comparison and increases the scale in the first formula. A rate change alone does not specify which comparison is intended.]{.key-statement} Could the measured CV itself mostly reflect drift rather than private spike variability? Supplementary Notes test this. Let $\lambda(t)=\bar\lambda+aB(t)$ during a fixation of length $T$, with the rate changes small relative to $\bar\lambda$. For a Brownian path starting at zero, the expected time averaged squared position is $DT$, and the expected squared time mean is $2DT/3$. Subtracting gives the expected within-segment position variance $DT/3=2DT/6$: $$ \mathbb E\!\left[\frac1T\int_0^T(B(t)-\bar B)^2dt\right] =\frac{DT}{3}. $$ The second term follows from $\mathbb E[B(t)B(s)]=2D\min(t,s)$ and $T^{-2}\int_0^T\int_0^T2D\min(t,s)\,dt\,ds=2DT/3$. Expanding $1/(\bar\lambda+aB)$ to first order gives $1/\bar\lambda-aB/\bar\lambda^2$. Dividing its standard deviation by its mean then gives $$ \mathrm{CV}_{\rm drift}\simeq \frac{|a|}{\bar\lambda}\sqrt{\frac{2DT}{6}}. $$ With the supplement's values $a=1/15$ spikes/(s arcmin), $2D=100$ arcmin$^2$/s, $T=0.5$ s, and $\bar\lambda=80$ Hz, this is about $0.0024$, well below the OMN CV near 0.07. These are an order of magnitude check, not a fitted diffusion constant for the whole model. Since one degree is 60 arcmin, that $2D$ equals $0.0278$ deg$^2$/s, or $D=0.0139$ deg$^2$/s.[^p2-cv-drift] ## The figures test shared drive, diffusion, and the full circuit model {#sec:EYE-FIGURES} The five figures address different steps. Their agreement is easier to assess when those questions remain separate.
{{block:tbl:EYE-FIGURE-GUIDE}}
The most useful supplemental comparisons are Extended Data Fig. 1 for individual uncertainty, Fig. 2 for noise subtraction and its simulated control, Fig. 3 for feedback, Fig. 4 for a no-central-drive control, and Fig. 5 for the other monkey's fit. In the no-central-drive control, $\widehat\chi=-0.09\pm0.22$ is compatible with zero. That negative estimate is sampling variation. Figures 6–8 document cell classification, segment sampling, and a rank correlation check. Figure 9 shows the heterogeneous model parameters. Figure 10 separates spiking noise passed directly to the output from spiking noise that drives diffusion inside the integrator: internal stochastic spikes remain in the latter comparison. Its caption reports little direct output-noise effect beyond 50 ms.[^p2-supp-figures]

## The evidence places shared drive upstream without identifying one circuit {#sec:EYE-LIMITS} The data and model answer different questions about where the drive originates: - The common variance estimate supports a drive upstream of OMNs, given the calibration and noise assumptions. - The MSD comparison supports a command that accumulates variation over the measured interval, rather than stationary white noise passed through a decaying muscle filter. - The circuit model shows that integrator noise with plausible parameters can generate such a command and explain its filtered amplitude and timing. Those results do not uniquely locate the noise inside integrator neurons. Two missing tests limit that conclusion: - No integrator neurons were recorded in this study. - No selective change of that circuit tested whether it was necessary for drift. [Noisy inputs to the integrator, or an already diffusive upstream signal, remain possible. The authors make this distinction in the Discussion and explicitly in their peer review response. Several combinations of neuron count, variability, and synaptic time constant can also fit an amplitude, so matching one curve does not uniquely recover those parameters.]{.key-statement}[^p2-localization] The study's empirical scope is horizontal motion during these fixation segments in two animals. Visual tasks, feedback, and other sources of input can alter the statistics. Its contribution to the connection with the 2012 theory is more precise: a continuous memory can diffuse internally, while a mechanical output of that memory looks smooth and superdiffusive at shorter lags. To compare a memory theory with behavior, the mapping from stored value to measured movement is part of the calculation. [^p2-network]: Ben-Shushan, N., Shaham, N., Joshua, M., & Burak, Y. (2022). *Fixational drift is driven by diffusive dynamics in central neural circuitry*. Nature Communications, 13, 1697. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-022-29201-y). Main pp. 10–11, “Oculomotor integrator network,” Eqs. 23–27; Supplementary Information, p. 13, Extended Data Fig. 9. [^p2-motor]: Ben-Shushan, N., Shaham, N., Joshua, M., & Burak, Y. (2022). *Fixational drift is driven by diffusive dynamics in central neural circuitry*. Nature Communications, 13, 1697. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-022-29201-y). Main p. 11, “OMN activity and actual eye position,” Eqs. 28–33 and simulation parameters; p. 6, Fig. 3 caption, private OMN comparison. [^p2-feedback]: Ben-Shushan, N., Shaham, N., Joshua, M., & Burak, Y. (2022). *Fixational drift is driven by diffusive dynamics in central neural circuitry*. Nature Communications, 13, 1697. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-022-29201-y). Main pp. 7, 9, 11, “Visual feedback,” Eq. 34; Supplementary Information, pp. 4–5 and p. 9, Extended Data Fig. 3. Some supplement cross references use earlier figure/equation numbers. Page 5 also mentions 15K integrator neurons, whereas final main Methods specify 30,000. This guide uses final main paper numbering and its main simulation parameters. [^p2-cv]: Ben-Shushan, N., Shaham, N., Joshua, M., & Burak, Y. (2022). *Fixational drift is driven by diffusive dynamics in central neural circuitry*. Nature Communications, 13, 1697. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-022-29201-y). Main p. 11, “Sub-Poisson spike trains,” Eq. 35 and integrator variability specification. The interval-sum derivation expands the construction given there. [^p2-scaling]: Ben-Shushan, N., Shaham, N., Joshua, M., & Burak, Y. (2022). *Fixational drift is driven by diffusive dynamics in central neural circuitry*. Nature Communications, 13, 1697. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-022-29201-y). Main p. 6, Eq. 1 and its parameter discussion; peer review file, p. 23, changes in slope, synaptic time constant, and neuron count. The absolute versus fractional slope distinction is the guide's dimensional interpretation of the printed normalization ambiguity, connected to the guide’s diffusion and information calculations. [^p2-cv-drift]: Ben-Shushan, N., Shaham, N., Joshua, M., & Burak, Y. (2022). *Fixational drift is driven by diffusive dynamics in central neural circuitry*. Nature Communications, 13, 1697. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-022-29201-y). Supplementary Information, pp. 2–3, “Contribution of oculomotor state to the CV of OMNs,” Eqs. S3–S6. Intermediate covariance integrals and numerical evaluation are expanded here. [^p2-supp-figures]: Ben-Shushan, N., Shaham, N., Joshua, M., & Burak, Y. (2022). *Fixational drift is driven by diffusive dynamics in central neural circuitry*. Nature Communications, 13, 1697, Supplementary Information, pp. 7–14, Extended Data Figs. 1–10. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-022-29201-y). The no-central-drive result is Extended Data Fig. 4, p. 10. The output-noise comparison is Extended Data Fig. 10, p. 14. [^p2-localization]: Ben-Shushan, N., Shaham, N., Joshua, M., & Burak, Y. (2022). *Fixational drift is driven by diffusive dynamics in central neural circuitry*. Nature Communications, 13, 1697. [DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-022-29201-y). Main pp. 7, 9, Discussion; peer review file, pp. 12–13, distinction between recording-based upstream localization and the integrator hypothesis.

paragraphs.text: <!-- vale ai-tells.ExplainerHeadings = YES -->

<!-- vale ai-tells.CataphoricForecasting = NO --> <!-- vale ai-tells.VerbTricolon = NO --> The subject is neuroscience: how groups of nerve cells represent information used in memory, eye control, and navigation. The three papers examine mathematical models that store a quantity such as an angle, eye movements and neural activity recorded in macaque monkeys, and location-dependent neural activity recorded in rodents and bats. [They ask how activity can retain a value, how an internal fluctuation can move the eyes, and why a cell can respond at several separate locations.]{.key-statement} <!-- vale ai-tells.VerbTricolon = YES --> <!-- vale ai-tells.CataphoricForecasting = YES -->

<!-- vale ai-tells.BareHolds = NO --> A remembered direction must remain useful after its cue disappears. The eyes must hold an angle while an animal looks at a target. A moving animal must keep track of where it is. These tasks depend on groups of [[**neuron**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}s, the brain's signaling cells]{.definition-explanation}, whose electrical signals are brief and variable. Computational and systems neuroscience studies how these cells and their interactions support such behavior. Mathematical models connect assumptions about cells and their interactions to predictions. Recordings test those predictions against neural activity and movement. <!-- vale ai-tells.BareHolds = YES -->

Burak and Fiete (2012) study short-term memory for a continuous quantity, such as a direction or eye angle. A proposed mechanism is that interacting neurons keep activity going after the original input ends. [Yet the remembered value can change while the activity persists.]{.key-statement} The problem is to explain how the properties of the cells and their connections set the rate of this loss of accuracy.

<!-- vale ai-tells.VerbTricolon = NO --> The authors analyze a network with a continuous family of persistent activity patterns, each representing a different value. Each cell sends signals at random times. They use an approximation for small fluctuations to derive how these signals move the stored value, compare the calculation with network simulations, and relate the motion to the best accuracy possible when estimating the stored value from those signals. <!-- vale ai-tells.VerbTricolon = YES -->

<!-- vale ai-tells.EmDashUsage = NO --> [Their central result is a lower bound: the uncertainty in reading the network's current value limits how slowly that value can wander.]{.key-statement} Under the model's assumptions, the variance of the memory error grows with storage time. Reading for longer also has diminishing benefit because the state continues moving during observation. This gives a benchmark for evaluating proposed memory circuits and their recall errors. It applies to the analyzed family of continuous-state memory models, with the required noise assumptions and no external signal anchoring the value. Chapters 3–6 develop the [diffusion calculation](../chapters/ch-memory-dynamics.html), its long-delay behavior, the [information bound](../chapters/ch-memory-information.html), and the limits of [readout](../chapters/ch-memory-readout.html).[^orientation-memory] <!-- vale ai-tells.EmDashUsage = YES -->

<!-- vale ai-tells.BareReaches = NO --> <!-- vale ai-tells.FormalTransitions = NO --> [Even while gaze is held on a stationary target, the eyes move smoothly and irregularly between brief, rapid movements. This smooth motion is called [**fixational drift**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}.]{.definition-explanation} It changes the image reaching the [[**retina**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}, the light-sensitive tissue at the back of the eye]{.definition-explanation}. Understanding its source is therefore part of understanding the visual signals the brain receives. [Ben-Shushan and colleagues (2022) ask whether the motion begins mainly in muscles or in neural commands sent to them.]{.key-statement} <!-- vale ai-tells.FormalTransitions = YES --> <!-- vale ai-tells.BareReaches = YES -->

They reanalyze recordings from 57 neurons that send commands to eye muscles in two macaques, paired with precise eye-position measurements. They first calibrate the relation between each cell's activity and larger eye movements. They then use it during fixation to compare the movement predicted from one cell with the measured movement. A separate circuit model tests whether a wandering stored eye-position command could explain the movement's amplitude and time dependence.

<!-- vale ai-tells.EmDashUsage = NO --> <!-- vale ai-tells.ParallelStaccato = NO --> For 350-millisecond intervals, their analysis estimates that about 82% of horizontal displacement variance comes from a common source before the final motor neurons, assuming the fitted movement relation also holds during fixation and the relevant noise contributions do not vary together. This supports a central neural contribution to drift. The memory-circuit model provides a possible explanation of that contribution, linking an internal storage error to observable behavior. The recordings do not uniquely locate the noise inside that memory circuit. Chapters 7–9 separate the [shared-drive inference](../chapters/ch-eye-drift.html), the [timing of drift](../chapters/ch-eye-timing.html), and the [proposed circuit mechanism](../chapters/ch-eye-circuit.html).[^orientation-eye] <!-- vale ai-tells.ParallelStaccato = YES --> <!-- vale ai-tells.EmDashUsage = YES -->

<!-- vale ai-tells.EmptyPaddingStacked = NO --> <!-- vale ai-tells.FormalTransitions = NO --> [A [**place cell**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} in the [**hippocampus**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}, a brain region involved in memory and navigation, becomes more active in particular locations.]{.definition-explanation} [Each connected region of elevated activity is a [**place field**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}.]{.definition-explanation} Small environments encouraged a picture of one smooth field per cell. Larger environments reveal multiple fields with widely varying sizes and shapes. [Mainali, Azeredo da Silveira, and Burak (2025) ask whether one statistical account can explain this variety across species and spatial dimensions.]{.key-statement} <!-- vale ai-tells.FormalTransitions = YES --> <!-- vale ai-tells.EmptyPaddingStacked = YES -->

Their model gives each cell a smooth random function of location and allows activity where that function exceeds a threshold. The authors derive predictions for the resulting regions, simulate the model, and compare it with existing rodent and bat recordings from one-, two- and three-dimensional environments. Parameters fitted to field sizes and their spatial arrangement also support further tests of field shapes and connectedness.

<!-- vale ai-tells.EmDashUsage = NO --> <!-- vale ai-tells.ParallelStaccato = NO --> The model explains different size distributions across dimensions and predicts additional features, such as multiple peaks within a field and inactive holes surrounded by activity. This makes irregular spatial responses quantitatively understandable and supports a common statistical description across the examined settings. Such statistics can arise when cells combine many inputs through largely random connections. The study does not directly measure those connections. Chapters 10–12 develop the [spatial model](../chapters/ch-place-fields.html), its [size and shape predictions](../chapters/ch-place-sizes.html), and the [tests and circuit interpretation](../chapters/ch-place-tests.html). They distinguish exact predictions, limiting approximations and empirical comparisons.[^orientation-place] <!-- vale ai-tells.ParallelStaccato = YES --> <!-- vale ai-tells.EmDashUsage = YES -->

<!-- vale ai-tells.CataphoricForecasting = NO --> <!-- vale ai-tells.FormalTransitions = NO --> <!-- vale ai-tells.ServesAsDodge = NO --> <!-- vale ai-tells.VerbTricolon = NO --> The three contributions therefore have different meanings: a mathematical constraint on memory models, evidence about the source of eye movement, and a statistical explanation of spatial activity. Together they show how a representation can be described, maintained and related to behavior. Combining all three in one biological circuit remains a further research question, developed in [Chapter 13](../chapters/ch-synthesis.html). <!-- vale ai-tells.VerbTricolon = YES --> <!-- vale ai-tells.ServesAsDodge = YES --> <!-- vale ai-tells.FormalTransitions = YES --> <!-- vale ai-tells.CataphoricForecasting = YES -->

<!-- vale ai-tells.AnthropomorphicCognition = NO --> The guide assumes undergraduate calculus, basic probability, and linear algebra. Neuroscience terms and the required stochastic-process, information, filtering, and random-field ideas are taught where needed. The reading path builds from the signals to the models and then their tests: <!-- vale ai-tells.AnthropomorphicCognition = YES -->
<!-- vale ai-tells.EmDashUsage = NO -->

**Chapters 1–2:** establish [neural signals and variability](../chapters/ch-foundations.html), then [persistence and accumulated error](../chapters/ch-persistence.html). <!-- vale ai-tells.EmDashUsage = YES --> <!-- vale ai-tells.EmDashUsage = NO --> <!-- vale ai-tells.VerbTricolon = NO -->

**Chapters 3–6:** derive memory diffusion, its long-delay behavior, the information bound, and readout. <!-- vale ai-tells.VerbTricolon = YES --> <!-- vale ai-tells.EmDashUsage = YES --> <!-- vale ai-tells.EmDashUsage = NO -->
**Chapters 7–9:** follow the eye study from shared-drive evidence through timing to a circuit model. <!-- vale ai-tells.EmDashUsage = YES --> <!-- vale ai-tells.VerbTricolon = NO -->
**Chapters 10–12:** develop spatial maps, their size predictions, and tests of their shapes and possible origins. <!-- vale ai-tells.VerbTricolon = YES -->
**Chapter 13:** connect the results and compare related work.
<!-- vale ai-tells.EmptyPadding = NO --> For a path focused on particular papers: <!-- vale ai-tells.EmptyPadding = YES -->
**Memory and eye drift:** follow chapters 1 through 9 in order. <!-- vale ai-tells.EmDashUsage = NO -->
**Place fields:** read the two foundations chapters and then chapters 10–12. The spatial calculation does not require the readout derivation in chapter 6. <!-- vale ai-tells.EmDashUsage = YES -->

The Glossary gives short definitions for lookup after their first explanation. The References section gives full source details. The original paper figures are discussed by number and can be inspected in the linked PDFs.
After the foundations, the [guide map](../chapters/ch-persistence.html#fig-foundations-paper-map) shows the three paper questions together.

On a first reading, follow the main text, figures, assumptions, and results. The expandable notes preserve longer calculations and extensions. Open one when you want to check the steps behind a result. The explanations needed for the next section remain in the main text.

<!-- vale ai-tells.EmDashUsage = NO --> Chapters 3–6 explain [how interacting neurons can retain a value while random spike timing changes it.]{.key-statement} Their treatment of the Burak and Fiete appendix separates three parts of each substantial topic: <!-- vale ai-tells.EmDashUsage = YES -->
<!-- vale ai-tells.VerbTricolon = NO -->

**Neural mechanism:** which cells and signals interact, what changes, and which features are assumptions of the model. For readout, this part also states what an observer can measure and which value it must estimate. <!-- vale ai-tells.VerbTricolon = YES --> <!-- vale ai-tells.VerbTricolon = NO -->
**Mathematical derivation:** the general tool, its conditions, and the calculation after neural quantities are assigned to the symbols. <!-- vale ai-tells.VerbTricolon = YES -->
**Interpretation:** what the result predicts about memory or readout, and what its assumptions leave unresolved.

<!-- vale ai-tells.StackedAnaphora = NO --> [An equation that specifies how a cell responds belongs to the model. A derivation works out what follows from that choice.]{.key-statement} <!-- vale ai-tells.StackedAnaphora = YES -->

<!-- vale ai-tells.FormalTransitions = NO --> For example, a spike can disturb several cells' activity. The circuit's interactions remove some changes, while others leave the represented angle displaced. Linear algebra calculates which part survives. Probability gives the spread of that displacement. The result then predicts how quickly memory errors accumulate in this model. The mathematical tools also apply to other systems, but this neural prediction depends on the circuit and spike statistics used in the calculation. <!-- vale ai-tells.FormalTransitions = YES -->

The same distinction matters for readout. A calculation of the best possible estimate sets a benchmark under specified access to neural signals. Establishing that an animal's neurons implement the assumed computation requires separate evidence.

<!-- vale ai-tells.FigurativeHolds = NO --> For a first conceptual pass, read the mechanism, inspect the displayed result and its variables, then read the interpretation. Follow the mathematical derivation when you want to understand why the result holds or calculate with it. Assumptions remain part of both readings. <!-- vale ai-tells.FigurativeHolds = YES -->

<!-- vale ai-tells.AnthropomorphicCognition = NO --> The [PNAS appendix](https://www.pnas.org/action/downloadSupplement?doi=10.1073%2Fpnas.1117386109&file=Appendix.pdf) supplies both neural-model choices and mathematical arguments. This map links its seven sections to the guide's explanations. Page links open the local copy. The guide sometimes uses an equivalent teaching derivation and identifies source inconsistencies beside the affected calculation. <!-- vale ai-tells.AnthropomorphicCognition = YES -->

<!-- vale ai-tells.AnthropomorphicCognition = NO --> Examples chosen for the guide distinguish independent from shared fluctuations, complete from limited access to neural signals, and exact formulas from approximations for rare fields. Their numbers are checked separately from the published experimental measurements. A teaching reconstruction is labeled when its simplified model differs from the paper's full model. <!-- vale ai-tells.AnthropomorphicCognition = YES -->

<!-- vale ai-tells.RestatementMarkers = NO --> The guide explains how to interpret the experiments and their figures. It does not rerun the original animal recordings, data processing, or full neural-network simulations. [A successful numerical check of a probability identity is different from an independent reproduction of a paper's empirical result.]{.key-statement} Related work is selected to clarify the assumptions and alternatives rather than to claim an exhaustive literature search. <!-- vale ai-tells.RestatementMarkers = YES -->

Throughout the guide, $D$ denotes the [[**diffusion coefficient**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}, which sets how quickly uncertainty spreads]{.definition-explanation}. In the basic one-dimensional model, $D$ is constant, neither direction is favored, and no boundary limits the motion. Its [[**mean squared displacement**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} (MSD), the average squared change in the represented coordinate after elapsed time $t$]{.definition-explanation}, is $2Dt$. [Chapter 2](../chapters/ch-persistence.html#sec-foundations-diffusion) explains this model and its assumptions.
The other recurring symbols are:
$d$: spatial dimension.
$\theta$: the represented coordinate in the memory chapters.
$q$: the normalized threshold in the place-field chapters, called $\theta$ in that paper.
$C$: the spatial covariance in the place-field chapters.
The copies are the published versions. Supporting information is linked separately.
<!-- vale ai-tells.EmDashUsage = NO -->

**Burak and Fiete (2012):** [Paper PDF](../papers/burak-fiete-2012-persistent-activity.pdf) and [20-page supporting information PDF](../papers/burak-fiete-2012-persistent-activity-si.pdf). *Fundamental limits on persistent activity in networks of noisy neurons*. PNAS, 109(43), 17645–17650. [Published DOI](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1117386109). The local main PDF uses the six-page Early Edition layout, so PDF page locators run from 1 to 6. <!-- vale ai-tells.EmDashUsage = YES --> <!-- vale ai-tells.VerbTricolon = NO -->

**Ben-Shushan, Shaham, Joshua, and Burak (2022):** [Paper PDF](../papers/ben-shushan-2022-fixational-drift.pdf), [supplementary notes and figures PDF](../papers/ben-shushan-2022-supplement-1.pdf), and [open peer review PDF](../papers/ben-shushan-2022-supplement-2.pdf). *Fixational drift is driven by diffusive dynamics in central neural circuitry*. Nature Communications, 13, 1697. [Published DOI](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-022-29201-y). Ben-Shushan and Shaham contributed equally. <!-- vale ai-tells.VerbTricolon = YES --> <!-- vale ai-tells.EmDashUsage = NO -->

**Mainali, Azeredo da Silveira, and Burak (2025):** [Paper and STAR Methods PDF](../papers/mainali-2025-universal-statistics.pdf) and [supplementary figures and Methods S1–S4 PDF](../papers/mainali-2025-supplement.pdf). *Universal statistics of hippocampal place fields across species and dimensionalities*. Neuron, 113(7), 1110–1120.e3. [Published DOI](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.neuron.2025.01.017). The main PDF has a cover before the article. Guide citations distinguish printed and PDF page numbers when needed. <!-- vale ai-tells.EmDashUsage = YES -->

The supporting-information copies preserve their original formulas. The guide identifies apparent inconsistencies in several printed intermediate equations beside the affected calculations and follows an explicitly shown derivation. Such observations are independent mathematical checks, not author-confirmed corrections.
<!-- vale ai-tells.EmDashUsage = NO -->
<!-- vale ai-tells.EmDashUsage = YES -->
<!-- vale ai-tells.ContrastiveFormulas = NO --> <!-- vale ai-tells.EmDashUsage = NO --> <!-- vale ai-tells.SemicolonUsage = NO -->
<!-- vale ai-tells.SemicolonUsage = YES --> <!-- vale ai-tells.EmDashUsage = YES --> <!-- vale ai-tells.ContrastiveFormulas = YES -->
<!-- vale ai-tells.EmDashUsage = NO -->
<!-- vale ai-tells.EmDashUsage = YES -->

<!-- vale ai-tells.EmptyPadding = NO --> Looking steadily at a small spot does not hold the eye perfectly still. [Between brief, rapid movements called [**microsaccades**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}, the eye makes a small, smooth, irregular movement called fixational drift.]{.definition-explanation} [Does this movement begin as noise in the muscles, or does the brain send a changing command to them?]{.key-statement} Ben-Shushan and colleagues answer this in two stages. Their recordings support a large shared drive upstream of the motor neurons. Their model then proposes a particular source: random motion of the eye position stored in a memory circuit.[^p2-question] <!-- vale ai-tells.EmptyPadding = YES -->
